detail.title: Still Can’t Tell:  A Close Replication of “Fooled Twice: People Cannot Detect Deepfakes But Think They Can”

keywords.keywords: NeuroscienceBehavioral neuroscienceCognitive neuroscienceArtificial intelligenceArtificial intelligence applicationsSocial sciencesPsychology

detail.abstract: Videos manipulated by deep-learning mechanisms (deepfakes) pose societal challenges through misinformation and fraud. Previous research found that people struggle to detect deepfakes and overestimate their detection ability. As deepfake technology has become more prevalent, it remains unclear whether these findings hold. In a preregistered online experiment (N = 373), we replicated a previous experiment by Köbis, Doležalová, & Soraperra (2021) and extended it by examining the role of AI literacy. Detection accuracy remained only slightly above chance, and participants continued to default to judging videos as real, albeit less so than in the original study, suggesting a weakening of the seeing-is-believing heuristic. Moment-to-moment overconfidence persisted, but incentivized overall performance estimates were better calibrated than in the original study. Neither awareness messages nor financial incentives improved accuracy, though both reduced overconfidence. Greater AI familiarity was associated with higher confidence but not better detection, suggesting it fosters a false sense of immunity rather than genuine protection. Our findings imply that human ability to detect deepfakes with the “naked eye” has not improved sufficiently to eliminate the need for safeguards at the system and user interface levels.

title: Post-materialism under Threat: Insecurity and Middle-class Value Shifts in East Asia (Preprint; Accepted for Publication in Sociology Compass, Forthcoming)

detail.title: Post-materialism under Threat: Insecurity and Middle-class Value Shifts in East Asia (Preprint; Accepted for Publication in Sociology Compass, Forthcoming)
detail.abstract: Does economic development drive a shift toward post-materialist values, and is middleclass identity central to this transition? Answering these questions is critical because even the United States, which supports Inglehart's argument in the beginning also faces strong materialism and globalization backlash. To explore these questions in an era of rising anti-globalization sentiment, this study revisits Inglehart's post-materialism theory and Brym's geopolitical hypothesis, analyzing data from three World Values Survey waves (2005-2022) across four East Asian countries. Using logistic regression with fixed effects and a Hierarchical Logit Model, we find that economic development partially fosters post-materialist shifts, but rising unemployment reinforces materialist values more than economic inequality. Younger and older generations, especially in China, show strong support for national defense, while class identity has an ambiguous effect. These findings suggest that political elites may mobilize generational rather than class-based support to address economic challenges. In an era of heightened geopolitical tensions, East Asian countries increasingly prioritize materialist values and national defense, reflecting collective insecurity. Post-materialist advocacy by the middle class may thus be a situational response to globalization rather than a universal trend.

title: Oil–VIX States as Conditional Signals for Cross-Asset Allocation

detail.title: Oil–VIX States as Conditional Signals for Cross-Asset Allocation
detail.abstract: This paper studies joint oil-volatility states as predictive conditioning variables for cross-asset returns. Using weekly equal-weighted class portfolios constructed from an 81-asset universe over 1990-2026, the paper combines event studies, pre-trend diagnostics, local projections, entry-versus-persistence decompositions, threshold-stability tests, factor decomposition, and a continuous specification with standardized oil, VIX, residual OVX, and an oil×VIX interaction. The preferred interpretation is predictive rather than causal: joint oil-VIX states summarize evolving macro-financial conditions rather than exogenous shocks. The paper classifies three non-trivial regimes: high-oil-high-VIX (HH), high-oil-low-VIX (HL), and low-oil-high-VIX (LH). Three results stand out. First, regime entries are rarely surprises: HH and LH follow equity drawdowns, while HL follows positive pre-entry momentum. Second, oil, market volatility, and oil-specific volatility each add information, with the oil×VIX interaction most negative for government bonds, credit, and later developed-market equities. Third, discrete regimes remain useful economically: HH is a two-stage stress state, HL resembles late-cycle rotation, and LH behaves as crash/stabilization with earlier fixed-income normalization. The framework is best read as a conditional allocation map rather than a fully validated trading rule.

detail.abstract: A self-built systematic equity strategy on U.S. large-capitalisation stocks reported a gross out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of approximately 1.3-a figure suggestive of genuine skill. This paper treats that figure as a claim to be audited rather than trusted. Running the identical model under three configurations that each differ in exactly one element, I decompose the apparent edge into its sources and test it with the skill metric appropriate to a cross-sectional ranking strategy. Three lines of evidence converge. First, by the rank information coefficient, the model has no detectable ability to order future returns in any configuration, and the survivorship-biased universe holds no skill advantage over a point-in-time one. Second, the survivor universe attains its higher Sharpe while holding fewer names, so its advantage lies in which companies it contains-the index's eventual winners-rather than in forecasting. Third, a decomposition of realised Sharpe attributes the largest gap to the universe correction (a point estimate of about 0.62, directionally consistent but, given the sampling uncertainty of Sharpe ratios over seven years, not statistically distinguishable from zero). What performance survives correction is marginal at best and negative under realistic trading costs. The headline Sharpe ratio was a property of a winner-selected universe, not evidence of forecasting ability.

detail.abstract: This study examines the connection between the investor sentiment and behavioral drivers and the performance of the Saudi financial market with a specific reference to the Tadawul All Share Index (TASI). The designed study employs a quantitative research strategy in which survey data are measured using a predefined questionnaire distributed among 100 respondents among individual and institutional investors, past trading volume and TASI returns in January 2025 - April 2025. The results demonstrate that investor sentiment plays a meaningful role in making investment decisions and there exists a strong correlation (Pearson coefficient of 0.947) where a positive investor sentiment results to higher level of trading activities and market volatility. Another factor, which was identified to impact investment decisions greatly, is behavioral biases like overconfidence and loss aversion with a correlation coefficient of 0.903. They also included the moderator, the emotional intelligence between the investor feeling and decision-making. The emotional intelligence had negative relationship with the investment decision although the relationship is not statistically significant (Beta = -0.320, p = 0.455). It does not reveal that Emotional Intelligence and investment decisions have a significant and positive correlation. The research supports the significance of the study of psychological determinants of investment behavior, implying that perceptions of investors and their emotions may cause market inefficiency, including bubble and crash. This study can be useful to investors and policymakers who seek to make the markets more stable and make better decisions because of pointing to the influence of sentiment on the market as well as the involvement of cognitive biases and emotional intelligence. The findings can be added to the collective research in the field of behavioral finance and especially in the environment of the Saudi financial market.

title: The Effectiveness of Climate Change Finance and The Importance of Capital Intensity: A Meso-Level Analysis of Climate Action Heterogeneity in British Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises

detail.title: The Effectiveness of Climate Change Finance and The Importance of Capital Intensity: A Meso-Level Analysis of Climate Action Heterogeneity in British Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises
detail.abstract: SME climate action priorities vary dramatically, yet sources of this heterogeneity remain poorly understood. We complement agent-focused research by examining underlying structural conditions-capital intensity, resource configurations, and organizational capabilities-that make climate action 'strategically' attractive for some SMEs while creating systematic barriers for others. Using the British Business Bank Survey data, we apply integrated resource-based view, dynamic capabilities theory, and external enablement framework with hierarchical variance decomposition across sectors. Our meso-level approach allows us to measure a real asset lock-in effect. We documented five heterogeneity dimensions: Industry resource configurations, capital intensity divide, climate action claims, firmographics and financing through growth expectations, and lifecycle with youngest firms clustering. Within-industry homogeneity confirms sectoral uniformity. Crucially, capital intensity determines green finance effectiveness heterogeneously: Bank loans work for non-capital-intensive industries with minimal abatement costs but fail for capital-intensive industries at substantially higher transition risk. Successful policies require sectoral coverage to address this bottleneck.

Knowledge management transforms raw data into actionable insights, enabling the bank to adapt to regulatory requirements, improve decision-making, and strengthen collaboration across branches. This report explores the importance of knowledge management systems, their dimensions, and applications, with a focus on how LANDBANK can leverage enterprise content management, knowledge networks, and intelligent techniques to enhance service delivery and organizational resilience.

title: The Cost of Capital of Biotechnology Firms (1997-2008): A Comparative Analysis of Intermediated and Neoliberal Capitalism Models -Answering a Research Question Left Open in 2012

detail.title: The Cost of Capital of Biotechnology Firms (1997-2008): A Comparative Analysis of Intermediated and Neoliberal Capitalism Models -Answering a Research Question Left Open in 2012
detail.abstract: This article re-analyses the cost of capital of biotechnology firms (BFs) over the pre-crisis 1997-2008 period, based on Tables 31-34 and 67-70 of the author's PhD dissertation (Tendil, 2012, University of Montpellier I, 1,064 BFs • 16 countries • Datastream 4.0 data). The 2012 dissertation explicitly left this line of analysis open on page 331-"this avenue will remain to be explored in future research"on the grounds that results on the cost of equity across capitalism models were "not very convincing". This article delivers precisely that deeper analysis by presenting and discussing three empirical elements recorded in the dissertation but not developed analytically in 2012: (i) the tests of difference of means on the cost of debt reported in Table 69 of the dissertation (intermediated vs ex-US neoliberal: t =-2.53, p = 0.0114; intermediated vs US: t =-5.08, p = 0.0000; ex-US neoliberal vs US: t =-6.05, p = 0.0000); (ii) the calculation of the cost of equity by CAPM under two variants (empirical premia computed by the dissertation and Damodaran premia); (iii) decomposition by firm size (+/-500 employees in 2008). Results confirm hypothesis HP16 of the dissertation for the cost of debt (significantly higher in neoliberal countries, particularly in the United States, than in intermediated countries) but qualify the hypothesis for the cost of equity: with Damodaran premia (4.74% for intermediated, 4.50% for neoliberal), the cost of equity is slightly higher in ex-US neoliberal countries (9.89%) than in intermediated countries (8%) or the US (9.69%), a result compatible with a nuanced reading of neoliberal capitalism models. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these pre-crisis results for the post-crisis 2008-2026 analysis of the financialisation of biotech intangible assets examined in Articles 5 and 8 of this series.

title: Unified Shrinkage for High-Dimensional Portfolio Choice
affiliations: Columbia University, , Columbia University, Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School and Independent

detail.title: Unified Shrinkage for High-Dimensional Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract: We develop a unified shrinkage framework for high-dimensional mean-variance portfolio choice. It jointly regularizes three objects that are typically treated separately: expected returns, the covariance matrix, and portfolio weights, nesting almost all widely used shrinkage and portfolio-combination rules as special cases, including mean shrinkage, covariance shrinkage, weight shrinkage toward naive diversification, and combinations thereof. For this general class, we derive analytical expressions for the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio and characterize the oracle shrinkage parameters that maximize it. We then construct feasible, data-driven tuning rules and show that they asymptotically attain the best Sharpe ratio available within the corresponding shrinkage class. Our results provide deep insights into the existing finding that covariance shrinkage is more important than mean shrinkage. While standard estimation of tuning parameters can fail in finite samples, refined tuning helps oracle rules achieve their expected performance. Our unified rule performs best or close to best among all existing rules across all datasets. Monte Carlo experiments and empirical applications to U.S., international, and anomaly-based datasets show that the proposed shrinkage rules deliver competitive out-of-sample performance, particularly in high-dimensional settings, even after accounting for transaction costs. Our paper provides a systematic foundation for portfolio shrinkage in practical portfolio construction under estimation risk.

title: Commodity-Linked Participation Rights (CLPRs / "Clippers"): An Exchange-cleared Market Architecture for Sovereign Critical Mineral Monetisation

detail.title: Commodity-Linked Participation Rights (CLPRs / "Clippers"): An Exchange-cleared Market Architecture for Sovereign Critical Mineral Monetisation

detail.abstract:
The energy transition requires an estimated $3 trillion in annual investment in critical minerals by 2030, yet sovereign borrowers who sit atop the world's lithium, cobalt, copper, and rare earth reserves face a structural paradox: immense real assets but weak credit profiles, leading to expensive debt and opaque bilateral deals that have historically exacerbated the resource curse. This paper proposes a new institutional market architecture-Commodity-Linked Participation Rights (CLPRs, or "Clippers")that enables sovereign producers to monetise future output without incurring debt, surrendering ownership, or falling prey to the "shadow power" documented by Blas and Farchy (2021). 

CLPRs are exchange-cleared, cash-settled participation rights sold via a transparent auction (e.g., CME Direct). Investors receive a fixed percentage of verified annual output; the sovereign retains full ownership and operational control. A two-tranche stabilisation mechanism (automatic production-period extension plus a multilateral Critical Mineral Stabilisation Fund) addresses commodity price volatility. A progressive enforcement ladder (Permanent Court of Arbitration, exchange suspension, multilateral sanctions) ensures compliance without violating sovereignty. A dedicated political economy section demonstrates how CLPRs mitigate opacity, asymmetric bargaining power, and off-market side payments-without overclaiming to "solve" corruption.

Using historical copper, lithium, and cobalt price series (2015-2025), we show that CLPRs can lower effective sovereign financing costs by 200-400 basis points compared to eurobonds, while reducing the probability of debt distress by more than half. The paper concludes with a phased implementation roadmap, a pilot proposal for Chile or Botswana, and a call for a multi-stakeholder working group involving the CME, the World Bank's IFC, and sovereign wealth funds.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel credit risk prediction framework for peer-to-peer (P2P) lending that draws theoretical inspiration from the Q-factor asset pricing model developed by Hou, Xue, and Zhang (2015, 2020). We propose the Q-Factor Health-Income Framework (QHIF), which maps traditional asset pricing factors—Investment, Profitability, Size, and Expected Growth—to analogous borrower characteristics: Leverage (debt-to-income ratios), Creditworthiness (FICO scores, income), Financial Capacity (total credit limits, account balances), and Credit Trajectory (inquiries, credit age). Additionally, we incorporate Health-Income Stability factors capturing employment stability, utilization volatility, and financial distress indicators. We evaluate our approach on 1,345,310 Lending Club loans using a stacking ensemble of LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, MLP neural networks, and TabNet deep learning models. Our methodology achieves an AUC of 72.97%, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art benchmark of 70.77% reported by Souadda et al. (2025). The stacking ensemble demonstrates a 2.20% improvement over prior work, validating the effectiveness of combining Q-factor inspired feature engineering with modern ensemble learning techniques. Our findings suggest that the theoretical foundations of asset pricing can be successfully translated to consumer credit risk assessment, offering a principled approach to feature selection and model design.

title: Federal Funds in Puerto Rico: The ARRA Experience and Lessons for Economic Recovery

detail.title: Federal Funds in Puerto Rico: The ARRA Experience and Lessons for Economic Recovery
detail.abstract: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (ARRA) injected $787 billion into the U.S. economy to counter the Great Recession. This paper examines how ARRA funds were allocated across spending types and sectors in Puerto Rico, how effectively they were administered by the local government, and their short-run macroeconomic impact. Puerto Rico received approximately $6.3 billion—equivalent to 6.5 percent of its 2009 nominal GDP—distributed across Awards, Entitlements, and Tax Relief. Federal oversight reports identified no systemic fraud but flagged deficiencies in project tracking, documentation, and data management. The ARRA coincided with the onset of a prolonged local economic contraction that began before the U.S. entered the Great Recession, offering a distinctive regional setting to assess how large federal transfers interact with such economic conditions. Using an interrupted time series model, the paper estimates that, absent the ARRA, Puerto Rico's real GDP would have declined by a cumulative 7.0 percent relative to its 2008 level by 2013. The observed decline was 3.0 percent. The findings indicate that federal spending can cushion a prolonged contraction in the short run but does not resolve underlying structural economic weaknesses.

detail.abstract: Power shortages are usually studied as missing inputs to production. I study a different margin. Recurring shortages induce durable backup-capital investment, and the emissions consequences depend on which technology becomes privately profitable. My central evidence is within India. After the 2021 coal-stock crunch, coal-heavy states show a persistent rise in grid-supplied energy and district power-sector CO2 that strengthens rather than fades through 2023, but this lock-in is attenuated in states with more generous pre-existing net-metering rules. South Africa's 2022-2024 loadshedding episode provides an external illustration of the alternative equilibrium, where shortages ran through diesel peakers but generous export credits coincided with rapid distributed-solar expansion. A calibrated backup-choice model explains why. Export credits monetize solar output outside outage hours, turning solar from an imperfect outage hedge into a generation asset with backup value, and flip the firm's private choice from diesel to grid-feeding solar. Electricity-reliability policy therefore changes the direction of induced capital, not only the level of capacity investment.

title: PIVOT: Bridging Black-Scholes Implied-Volatility and Price Objectives via Differentiable Jäckel Operator

detail.title: PIVOT: Bridging Black-Scholes Implied-Volatility and Price Objectives via Differentiable Jäckel Operator

declarations.funderStatement: Raeid Saqur is supported by the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) through the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) via Programme Grant [Grant No.\ UKRI1010: High order mathematical and computational infrastructure for streamed data that enhance contemporary generative and large language models] and the Vector Research Grant by the Vector Institute for AI, Canada.

detail.abstract: Modern option-learning systems operate in two coordinates: price space, where markets quote and no-arbitrage constraints are most naturally enforced, and implied volatility (IV) space, where volatility surfaces are smoothed, regularized, and evaluated. The bottleneck is interface, not approximation: Jäckel's seminal Let's Be Rational (LBR) solver already inverts the Black-Scholes price to machine precision efficiently. What is missing is a differentiable layer that preserves LBR in the forward pass and avoids backpropagating through its branch logic. Such a layer must also confront the unavoidable singularity of the inverse map in the low-vega regime, where ∂σ/∂P = 1/V diverges as V → 0. We close this gap with PIVOT, Price-Implied-Volatility Objective Translator. PIVOT keeps the LBR forward pass intact and supplies the backward pass by implicit differentiation through the smooth Black-Scholes/Black-76 price map, with an explicit gating contract: invalid domains return NaN, well-conditioned rows receive the exact 1/V gradient, and low-vega rows are attenuated rather than silently regularized. On a single H100, a fused Triton kernel reaches 1.79×10 9 IV/s at machine precision (9.3×10-14 max relative error vs. the reference C solver); end-to-end label generation sustains 48.9M/s on synthetic chains and 16.6M/s on SPX OptionMetrics. In a HyperIVstyle one-day reproduction on SPX, PIVOT-augmented objectives Pareto-dominate the baselines, reducing held-out price MAE by up to 43.4% and the strongest three-seed gated objective improving price MAE by 38.8% and IV MAE by 21.3% jointly; cross-asset results on RUT, VIX, and NDX show directional price-MAE gains of 40.1%, 24.2%, and 16.7%, while an ungated IV-roundtrip control collapses to a degenerate near-zero surface, confirming the gate as a correctness contract rather than a tuning knob.

title: Intellectual Property Law Firm Networks and Tax Haven Secrecy: Evidence from Exchange of Information on Request Agreements

detail.title: Intellectual Property Law Firm Networks and Tax Haven Secrecy: Evidence from Exchange of Information on Request Agreements
detail.abstract: We examine how intellectual property (IP) law firms facilitate multinational corporations' shifting of IP-related income to tax havens by exploiting haven secrecy, and whether global tax transparency initiatives constrain this impact. Analyzing U.S. patent assignment data, we find that companies transferring patents to havens are abnormally clustered through shared law firm links, implying that law firms disseminate specialized knowledge about exploiting haven secrecy. Companies are 64% more likely to assign patents to a tax haven when linked through a law firm to another company that has done so. Importantly, this linkage effect subsides after the implementation of the OECD's Exchange of Information on Request (EOIR), suggesting that improving transparency erodes the secrecy-based comparative advantage embedded in law firm networks. Economically, law-firm-facilitated patent transfers generate substantial cash tax savings, approaching $645 million over five years. Our evidence highlights both the importance of legal intermediaries and the disciplining role of transparency reforms.

title: Verifiable Agent Identity and Delegated Authority in Autonomous Payment Systems: A Trust Architecture for AI-Initiated Financial Transactions

detail.title: Verifiable Agent Identity and Delegated Authority in Autonomous Payment Systems: A Trust Architecture for AI-Initiated Financial Transactions
detail.abstract:
The emergence of autonomous payment agents capable of initiating, routing, and settling financial transactions introduces a fundamental challenge that existing payment infrastructure is not designed to address: how can counterparties, financial institutions, and regulatory systems verify that an artificial intelligence agent has been delegated legitimate authority to act on behalf of an identifiable principal within an enforceable scope of authorization? Existing identity and authorization frameworks—including OAuth, decentralized identity standards, and traditional financial authentication mechanisms—provide mechanisms for identity verification but lack a trust architecture for representing and validating delegated authority in autonomous financial environments.

Building on prior research on intelligent payment systems, autonomous financial execution, and governance frameworks for sovereign payment agents, this paper proposes a Verifiable Agent Identity (VAI) architecture comprising four interdependent components: (1) Agent Identity Credentials that encode authorization scope and provenance, (2) a distributed Agent Registry for credential lifecycle management, (3) a Policy Attestation Protocol enabling transaction-time verification of policy compliance, and (4) a Trust Envelope Framework supporting cross-jurisdictional recognition of agent credentials.

The framework is evaluated against representative deployment scenarios involving cross-border stablecoin settlement, autonomous treasury operations, and agentic commerce systems. The analysis demonstrates that verifiable identity and delegated authority represent foundational trust requirements for the responsible scaling of autonomous financial execution and cannot be treated as secondary governance concerns.

The paper argues that as AI systems increasingly participate in payment initiation and value transfer, financial infrastructure will require new trust mechanisms analogous to those that enabled identity and authentication in earlier generations of digital commerce. Accordingly, verifiable agent identity should be viewed as a critical architectural layer for next-generation intelligent payment systems and a priority area for future standards development, regulatory coordination, and industry adoption.

title: Market Expectations and Global Reactions: The Role of U.S. Presidential Election Betting Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Market Expectations and Global Reactions: The Role of U.S. Presidential Election Betting Markets
detail.abstract: Policies of the United States have a significant impact on the global economy and financial markets. As the ruling party determines the policies, U.S. Presidential Elections become one of the most significant and highly observed events all over the world. Investors constantly update their expectations in response to new information, and betting markets are involved as they provide probabilities of winning the election in real time, based on the current information. These probabilities affect the investors sentiment and their decisions within global markets. In this study, we analyse the association between U.S. election betting market probabilities and financial market movements. It examines various types of assets, such as global equity indices, Tesla stock and Bitcoin. We have applied statistical methods like abnormal return analysis and Lee-Mykland jump detection method, to analyse both gradual and extreme movements of the markets during the election. The findings indicate that financial markets react not only to the final results of the election but also to changes in winning probabilities throughout the election period. We have noticed that majority of world indices show negative responses in times of high political uncertainty, which also gives the evidence of extreme movements around major election events. These observations also demonstrated that it takes relatively short time span before markets start reacting when there are significant changes in candidates’ winning probabilities.

title: Price Competition and Managerial Delegation Under Partial Cooperation
affiliations: Institute for Economic Sciences

detail.title: Price Competition and Managerial Delegation Under Partial Cooperation
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes a three-stage Bertrand duopoly with partial cooperation and managerial delegation. In the first stage, each owner decides whether to hire a manager. In the second stage, owners who hire managers select their managers' incentive parameters. In the third stage, managers-or owners if no delegation occurs-simultaneously and independently set the firms' prices. The equilibrium is derived using backward induction under a subgame-perfect equilibrium. As a result, the paper shows that managerial delegation does not increase payoffs for either firm. This finding contrasts sharply with the Cournot case, where delegation is profitable, and highlights that the strategic value of delegation depends critically on the mode of competition.

detail.abstract: Sovereign credit rating agencies and corruption perception indices regularly assign materially different governance assessments to the same countries. This paper documents that divergence systematically across 48 rated sovereigns, identifies the mechanism, and draws three practical implications for investors, rating analysts, and ESG mandate designers. Using a symmetric two-equation design, we run identical governance variables simultaneously as predictors of sovereign rating notches and Transparency International CPI scores. The preferred specification uses 2012–2024 data (N=623), the period in which TI's methodology is time-comparable; results from the full 2005–2024 panel (N=936) are reported for reference. WGI Government Effectiveness is significantly associated with rating notches within country over time (β=+0.257, p<0.01) but not CPI scores. Government debt predicts ratings (β=−0.036, p<0.01) but not CPI. V-Dem Liberal Democracy predicts CPI marginally but not ratings. The association holds for Fitch and Moody's separately, arguing against a purely mechanical WGI input-transmission explanation, strengthens after 2008, is not mediated through fiscal variables, and temporally precedes rating changes at the one-year horizon. We term this the Governance Pricing Paradox. Three findings are directly actionable. First, ESG sovereign funds screening on CPI are partially screening for income level rather than governance quality — significant in the full panel but weakening to insignificance on TI's time-comparable post-2012 data, confirming that within-country CPI movements are not well explained by the variables that predict ratings. Second, a post-2008 structural break shows markets became measurably more sensitive to administrative capacity after the financial crisis; governance screens built on pre-crisis assumptions are mis-calibrated for the current environment. Third, political accountability deficits that markets discount over five years can become material credit risks over fifteen, as Venezuela's decade-long institutional deterioration preceding default illustrates. We propose a Dual-Axis Governance Framework separating Fiscal Governance (FGI) — what rating markets price — from Political Accountability (PAI) — what determines long-run institutional sustainability. The framework is applicable to ESG mandate design, rating agency methodology review, and sovereign debt risk assessment, and is consistent with the IMF's documented call for sovereign ESG methodology reform.

title: Policy Levers in Intellectual Property Law and the Right to Repair

detail.title: Policy Levers in Intellectual Property Law and the Right to Repair
detail.abstract: Recent developments in right to repair laws across multiple jurisdictions have intensified scrutiny of how far manufacturers may assert intellectual property (IP) rights post-sale. This article examines the right to repair movement and emerging legislative responses, focusing on three central developments: access to spare parts, disclosure of repair information, and lawful circumvention of technological protection measures. Setting aside mandatory supply of parts and tools, it argues that existing IP policy levers-exhaustion doctrine, a normative account of repair, and abuse of rights-cannot reliably expand the space for repair activities in the absence of a bespoke right to repair. This article then turns to Japan and contends that while adopting right to repair legislation would align with Japan's circular economy objectives, the threshold question is whether access barriers to repair comparable to those in other jurisdictions in fact arise to an extent that justifies rebalancing rights between IP holders and consumers.

title: Climate-Vulnerable Firms, Credit Supply, and Cascading Failures: An Agent-Based Model

detail.title: Climate-Vulnerable Firms, Credit Supply, and Cascading Failures: An Agent-Based Model
detail.abstract: We study the joint dynamics of firm and bank fragility under climate risk, decomposed into its physical and transition components, within a Greenwald-Stiglitz-type agent-based economy in which a population of heterogeneous firms interacts with a single aggregate bank through a credit market. The model embeds three climate-related channels: (i) a temperature-dependent damage function on output (physical risk); (ii) a carbon levy/permit mechanism that prices greenhouse-gas emissions (transition risk); and (iii) R&D investment that jointly raises productivity and lowers carbon intensity, so that the two risks interact endogenously with growth. We derive closed-form expressions for the bankruptcy probability, the optimal capital stock, and the Walrasian equilibrium interest rate, and we run agent-based simulations on the NGFS Net Zero 2050 pathway. Without a bank, physical risk dominates the output-growth losses while endogenous R&D pulls carbon intensity below its deterministic trend. With an active bank, the credit channel roughly doubles the macroeconomic cost of each climate channel relative to the accommodative-credit benchmark, and climate stress propagates into bank equity, bad debt, and cascading defaults rather than into the price of credit. Our aim is to reproduce stylised facts and identify emergent macroeconomic patterns rather than to forecast any specific economy: parameter values are empirically plausible (calibrated on French data where possible), and we transparently document the régime in which the endogenous default rate and interest rate settle at economically high values, leaving a finer quantitative calibration to subsequent work.

title: Working Paper:  "From Classical to Quantum: A Suggested Framework for Modeling Tax Evasion Behavior"
affiliations: American University of the Middle East (AUM)

detail.title: Working Paper:  "From Classical to Quantum: A Suggested Framework for Modeling Tax Evasion Behavior"
detail.abstract: This paper develops an innovative quantum cognition approach to explain tax evasion behavior. Conventional tax compliance theories, including deterrent theory and behavioral approach, generally apply classical probability assumption as well as assume constant preference of taxpayers. Empirical studies, however, show that taxpayer decisions are inconsistent, context specific, and socially determined in nature, sometimes even being influenced by ethical considerations. In response to such observations, this research takes a quantum probability perspective where taxpayer decisions are considered a dynamic and complex cognitive phenomenon featuring superposition, interference, and entanglement. Specifically, the paper creates a mathematical formalization with respect to tax compliance behavior that describes a cognitive state of a taxpayer represented by a vector in a Hilbert space, with compliance and evasion behaviors considered to occur simultaneously prior to a definite choice between the two. The paper elaborates the interference mechanism through which framing effects, social determinants, and cognitive conflict affect probabilities of tax compliance. In addition, formalization extends into a three-dimensional state space for partially compliant taxpayers' behavior as well as includes socially entangled tax decisions in a cognitive framework. By means of mathematical simulation and computation of the model, the paper reveals that the quantum cognition approach produces compliance probabilities that depend on context, exhibit non-linearity, and are socially related in ways beyond the capabilities of traditional econometrics methods. The result implies that tax compliance can be considered context-specific and non-probabilistic as a behavioral decision in nature. This study contributes to the literature in interdisciplinary research on tax compliance, behavioral economics, and quantum cognition. In terms of practical significance, the implication of this research includes not only the possibility of enhancing voluntary compliance through governmental enforcement but also through influencing cognitive and social contexts of taxpayer decisions.

title: Justified Envy Under Unilateral Substitutability

detail.title: Justified Envy Under Unilateral Substitutability
detail.abstract: Romm et al. (2024) show that in matching markets with contracts, if schools' choice functions are substitutable then the student-proposing deferred-acceptance/cumulative-offer process yields a stable allocation with no strong justified envy. They leave open whether the same conclusion continues to hold under unilateral substitutability in the sense of Hatfield and Kojima (2010). This paper gives a two-part answer. First, we give a two-student, one-school counterexample showing that unilateral substitutability together with irrelevance of rejected contracts is not enough: in our example, the cumulative-offer process outcome-which is in fact the unique stable allocationadmits justified envy in the strong-priority sense of Romm et al. (2024). Second, we show that the no-justified-envy conclusion is restored if schools' choice functions additionally satisfy the law of aggregate demand.

detail.title: Deepening Integration, Demanding Accountability: Key Takeaways from the 25th EAC Summit

publicationDetails.detailsText: The Platform Magazine, Volume 123, April 2026 Issue

detail.abstract:
The 25th Ordinary Summit of the East African Community (EAC), held in Arusha, Tanzania, on 7 March 2026 under the theme “Deepening Integration for Improved Livelihoods of EAC Citizens,” marked a significant moment in the evolution of regional integration in East Africa. As the apex decision-making organ of the Community, the Summit adopted a series of far-reaching resolutions aimed at addressing longstanding institutional, financial, and trade-related challenges that have hindered the realization of the objectives of the EAC Treaty. This article critically examines the key outcomes of the Summit and evaluates their potential impact on the future of regional integration.

The article explores four major developments emerging from the Summit. First, it analyses the transition of leadership within the Community, including the transfer of the Summit chairmanship from Kenya to Uganda and the appointment of a new Secretary General. Second, it assesses the progress reported in the reduction of non-tariff barriers (NTBs), the launch of the EAC Customs Bond, and the continued efforts to facilitate intra-regional trade. While acknowledging these achievements, the article argues that greater utilization of the Secretary General’s office is necessary to provide a more proactive and institutionalized mechanism for addressing NTBs as they arise.

Third, the article evaluates the adoption of a new funding framework designed to address persistent budgetary constraints that have affected key organs such as the East African Court of Justice and the East African Legislative Assembly. The Summit’s decision to link eligibility for senior regional positions to treaty compliance and financial contributions, coupled with the introduction of a revised contribution formula and sanctions regime, reflects a deliberate shift towards fiscal responsibility and institutional accountability. Fourth, the article considers other significant resolutions, including directives on treaty domestication, the political confederation process, and judicial appointments within the Community.

The article contends that the resolutions adopted at the 25th Summit signal a transition from symbolic commitments towards a more results-oriented model of regional governance. By emphasizing accountability, financial sustainability, and implementation, the Summit sought to confront some of the structural weaknesses that have historically undermined regional integration efforts. However, the success of these reforms will ultimately depend on the willingness of partner states to honour their commitments and translate Summit resolutions into concrete action.

The article concludes that the 25th EAC Summit has the potential to become a defining moment in the history of the Community. If effectively implemented, its resolutions could strengthen regional institutions, enhance economic integration, and advance the EAC’s vision of a prosperous, peaceful, and deeply integrated East Africa.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the dilemma of staying or leaving under conditions of war, occupation, and political repression through the lens of identity formation rather than purely moral or political frameworks. It argues that such decisions are deeply rooted in early autobiographical memory, place attachment, and collective narratives that shape the individual and collective sense of belonging. Drawing on theories of self-concept, social identity, collective memory, and diaspora studies, the paper proposes a three-layer analytical model: early identity formation structured by childhood memory; collective ethos and national narratives that moralise staying or legitimise leaving; and structural forces of power that redefine individuals as insiders or outsiders across contexts of homeland and exile. Through comparative references to Palestine and Vietnam, the paper illustrates how different peoples construct philosophies of endurance, resistance, and survival, while also highlighting generational divergences in exile. The study concludes that staying or leaving cannot be understood solely as acts of loyalty or betrayal, but as identity processes governed by memory, temporality, and the lived relationship to place.

title: The Direction of Value Flow: A Theory of Platform Fragility under AI Substitution
affiliations: Northeastern University

detail.title: The Direction of Value Flow: A Theory of Platform Fragility under AI Substitution
detail.abstract: Digital platforms built on user-generated content face a new kind of shock: generative AI substitutes directly for the interactions that give them value. Some have collapsed in the two years since ChatGPT's release while others in adjacent domains have remained stable. This heterogeneity-across platforms, and across user tiers within a platform-is not explained by accounts organized around AI's capability in different task domains. We develop an equilibrium theory in which fragility is governed by a structural feature of design: the degree to which value flows directionally, from higher-to lower-skilled users, rather than laterally among peers. The cascade threshold separating clean truncation from full collapse is strictly decreasing in this directionality, so more directional platforms collapse at lower AI reach. A second and more distinctive prediction concerns survivors: when the shock truncates a platform from below without collapsing it, the share of value carried by the peer channel rises for every remaining high-skill participant-a compositional reorganization that follows from the geometry of the matching technology rather than the model's asymmetric weights, and that a capability-only account cannot generate. A transient-overestimation mechanism produces hysteresis: a platform pushed into collapse by inflated early beliefs about AI does not recover when beliefs correct, because the empty platform is itself absorbing, and recovery requires coordinated re-entry of the whole surviving cohort. The theory yields falsifiable predictions that separate the directionality channel from the capability channel through within-platform tier variation, off-diagonal cross-platform comparisons, and compositional shifts in engagement.

title: Camouflage Optimization Algorithm: An adaptive Evolutionary Framework for Fast and Robust Convergence
affiliations: Adamas University, Adamas University, Adamas University, Kolkata and Adamas University, Kolkata

detail.title: Camouflage Optimization Algorithm: An adaptive Evolutionary Framework for Fast and Robust Convergence
detail.abstract: Nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithms have become essential tools for solving complex optimization problems across science and engineering. Techniques such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) draw inspiration from animal behaviour to intelligently balance exploration and exploitation as they navigate large search spaces. Although these algorithms have achieved notable success, they are not without limitations. Issues such as premature convergence, getting trapped in local optima, and difficulty adapting to rapidly changing environments can significantly reduce their performance, especially in real-world applications where problem landscapes are highly dynamic. To address these challenges, the Camouflage Optimization Algorithm (COA) is proposed as a fresh and biologically grounded alternative. COA takes inspiration from the remarkable camouflage abilities found in nature, where animals continuously adjust their colours, textures, and patterns to blend seamlessly with their surroundings, confuse predators, or gain a survival advantage. Translating this behaviour into a computational framework, COA introduces an adaptive search mechanism that allows candidate solutions to "blend" with their environment, improving their ability to escape local traps and explore the search space more effectively. This dynamic adaptation makes COA a promising approach for achieving more robust, flexible, and efficient optimization performance.

detail.abstract: This study investigates estimates a structural New Keynesian Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model for Algeria, grounded in the canonical framework of (Clarida et al., 1999). By utilizing the Unobserved Components-Dynamic Conditional Score (UC-DCS) framework in R, we successfully disentangle the permanent trend from the transitory output gap, explicitly accounting for the heavy-tailed shocks and outliers inherent in a rentier, oil-dependent state. Our Bayesian structural estimation in Stata reveals a high degree of intertemporal optimization within the Algeria economy, evidenced by a discount factor (β = 0.953) that aligns with the upper bounds of international benchmarks. This elevated value indicates that current inflation dynamics are predominantly driven by forward-looking expectations rather than purely historical inertia. Consequently, the effectiveness of the Bank of Algeria's monetary anchor is amplified by the expectational channel, with a posterior response coefficient (1/ψ) of 1.44, the authority successfully leverages the Taylor Principle to coordinate these anticipations. However, the interplay between high discount rates and structural rigidities (κ = 0.309) suggests that while the expectations-heavy nature of the aids stabilization, the underlying transmission remains sensitive to the persistent memory of exogenous shocks and hydrocarbon-driven fluctuations in the natural rate of interest.

detail.abstract: On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel coordinated an air attack on Iran. Market reactions were swift and reflected uncertainty over fuel and fertilizer movements in the Strait of Hormuz. In the weeks to follow, oil and fertilizer prices rose by nearly 50%. Predictions of corn prices for the year, likewise rose reflecting the potential cost increases. In this study, we attempt to quantify the potential economic impact while acknowledging the uncertainty over day-to-day changes in the war itself. Using USDA and futures price estimates from prior to and after the war, we incorporate these impacts into an equilibrium trade model and then use its outputs to generate economic impacts in an input-output model. Findings include: • US corn growers stand to lose $6 billion in revenues and $4 billion in additional costs for an approximate $6 billion loss in profits (producer surplus) and an additional $3 billion loss to workers in the US corn production industry. • Additional losses to the US economy along the corn supply chain amount to about $5 billion in lost revenue and an added $3 billion in lost sales related to general spending in the rest of the economy. • The total loss in sales related to the US corn supply chain amounts to about $13 billion, of which about $10 billion is a loss to US gross domestic product. • Losses to the state of Iowa would be approximately 15-20 percent of these losses based on Iowa's share of the US corn market.

detail.abstract:
In recent years, a novel but undervalued governance instrument has emerged that threatens the very foundations of American labor law: managerial power over the authoritative account of a firm's technological future. Extant labor doctrine takes a neutral position on the private ordering between employers and workers. Management's capacity to convince workers that their jobs depend on keeping labor costs low is virtually unchecked. Labor law lacks a mechanism and vocabulary to redistribute bargaining power in an era of future automation, leaving workers relatively powerless. 

This Article examines the legal implications of future-automation rhetoric. It advances a theoretical framework it calls epistemic power, which refers to the capacity of employers to control the authoritative content of facts material to workers’ decisions, under conditions in which workers have no independent mechanism to verify those facts. Applying this theoretical framework to labor law exposes the normative stakes of a governance regime that uses future automation to control workers, particularly those without union representation. This account reveals that the National Labor Relations Board has the statutory authority to regulate epistemic power and redistribute power back to workers. And yet, current labor doctrine permits employers to link future automation to workers’ protected right to organize during the election period without requiring the employer to substantiate their claims until after the votes have been cast. Future automation, including burgeoning generative artificial intelligence (AI), is distinctly perceived as inevitable; its rhetoric is thus particularly coercive. This Article proposes a doctrinal framework that calls for the equal distribution of bargaining power between labor and capital by requiring employers to substantiate their future automation statements when they are made, during the election window.

detail.abstract: Healthcare analytics, clinical pathway analysis, predictive modeling, and artificial intelligence applications require large-scale and well-structured datasets derived from routine hospital operations. However, hospital information systems often store diagnoses, procedures, reimbursement classifications, and hospitalization outcomes in heterogeneous formats that are difficult to integrate into analytical workflows. This article presents the Clinical Pathway Data Engineering Framework (CPDEF), a reproducible methodology for constructing machine learning-ready case-mix datasets from hospital information systems.CPDEF integrates ICD-10 diagnoses, ICD-9-CM procedures, INA-CBG classifications, and length-of-stay information into a standardized analytical repository. The framework was applied to 165,391 inpatient hospitalization episodes collected between November 2016 and April 2026 and produced a repository containing 32 standardized variables suitable for healthcare analytics and artificial intelligence applications. Validation confirmed the reproducibility, structural consistency, and machine learning readiness of the resulting dataset. CPDEF provides a transparent and scalable workflow for transforming heterogeneous hospital data into machine learning-ready analytical resources.Method highlights Provides a reproducible framework for constructing standardized case-mix datasets from hospital information systems.Integrates diagnoses, procedures, reimbursement classifications, and hospitalization outcomes into a unified analytical repository.Supports healthcare analytics, clinical pathway analysis, predictive modeling, and artificial intelligence applications.

detail.abstract: There is regular interest among farmers, agribusinesses, and policymakers concerning the competitiveness of food and agricultural industries. It has also been of great interest to economists and has been researched for nearly a century as detailed by Crespi and MacDonald (2022) and recently studied to great extent by the US Department of Agriculture (MacDonald, Dong, and Fuglie 2023). detail.abstract: This study investigates the contrasting impact of financial development on inequality in oil and gas-dependent countries compared to more diversified economies. The sample consists of developed and developing countries, with cross-sectional data averaged over the period 2013 to 2019. To ensure the robustness of the results and address potential endogeneity, the analysis employs a Two-Stage Least Squares (2SLS) approach, using creditor legal rights and the depth of credit information as instrumental variables. The findings reveal three main insights. First, oil and gas dependency, despite its direct inequality-reducing effect, weakens the equalizing role of financial development, leading to greater inequality in oil and gasdependent countries, and this pattern is robust across institutional and income-level groups. Second, the diminished inequality-reducing effect of financial development in oil and gasdependent countries, especially in higher and middle-institutional-quality, and higherincome countries, is driven by disruptions in the mechanisms through which financial development typically reduces inequality-namely, entrepreneurship and human capital. However, in lower-income, low-institutional-quality economies this pattern is more closely associated with broader resource-curse distortions. Third, beyond the effect of oil and gas dependency, this study contributes to the financial development-inequality literature by empirically documenting that the inequality-increasing and inequality-reducing mechanisms of financial development proposed in the theoretical literature can coexist. These Findings deepen our understanding of the channels through which financial development affects inequality in general and under the resource curse.

detail.abstract: Modern software delivery requires quality assurance that scales with development velocity. Manual test coordination, sequential test execution, and static risk assessment create bottlenecks that constrain release frequency and accumulate quality debt. This paper presents the K11tech Agentic AI QA System, a LangGraph-orchestrated multi-agent framework that automates the full CI/CD quality gate-from pull request analysis to defect filing-without requiring manual QA intervention for routine changes. A self-evaluation layer using DeepEval and RAGAS continuously audits the quality of the system's own LLM-generated outputs. detail.abstract:
Purpose - This study investigates the contributions of agriculture, industry, and services to Bangladesh’s economic growth, addressing controversies regarding their short- and long-run impacts within the framework of structural transformation.

Design/methodology/approach - Using annual time-series data from 1971–2020, the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach was employed to estimate both long-run elasticities and short-run dynamics. Complementary diagnostic and stability tests ensured robustness of the model.

Findings - Results confirm a strong long-run cointegrating relationship between GDP and the three sectors. Services emerged as the dominant driver of growth, industry contributed positively but moderately, and agriculture remained vital in both the short and long run. The error correction term indicated rapid adjustment toward equilibrium, underscoring resilience in Bangladesh’s growth process.

Research limitations - The study is limited to aggregate sectoral data, which may mask heterogeneity within subsectors. External shocks such as climate change and global trade disruptions were not explicitly modeled.

Originality/value - By jointly analyzing agriculture, industry, and services within a unified ARDL framework, this study reconciles econometric evidence with structural transformation theory, offering evidence-based insights for balanced sectoral development in Bangladesh.

title: How Long Does It Take to Sell Your Products?

detail.title: How Long Does It Take to Sell Your Products?
detail.abstract: We study the pricing problem of a seller with finite inventory over a finite sales horizon. Customers arrive according to a Poisson process and have valuations drawn from short-tailed, light-tailed, or heavy-tailed distributions, corresponding to the standard classes in Extreme Value Theory. Our focus is on the normalized time required to sell k out of q products in an asymptotic regime in which the sales horizon becomes large. Under optimal static pricing, we show that for short-tailed and light-tailed valuations, the time required to sell k products converges to zero, both in distribution and in expectation. For heavy-tailed valuations, by contrast, the limiting distribution is non-degenerate but exhibits a positive probability of unsold inventory. Under optimal dynamic pricing, we show that the time of the kth sale converges to an expression that involves a product of Beta random variables, whose parameters are determined by the tail class of the valuation distribution. In the light-tailed case, this reduces to the kth order statistic of a uniform distribution, implying that sales are asymptotically optimally balanced over the available horizon. For short-tailed and heavy-tailed valuations, the corresponding distributions are shifted slightly earlier and later, respectively, within the sales horizon. In addition, we show that sales times admit a natural interpretation on a logarithmic time scale, derive comparative statics, and demonstrate that, in general, static pricing cannot be said to be uniformly faster or slower than dynamic pricing. Our results address the question of what constitutes the "right time" to sell a product and provide practitioners with insights into expected sales patterns, which may contribute to greater compliance and trust in pricing software.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether caseload pressure changes appellate decision-making. Using 3.3 million Chinese civil appellate decisions from 2013 to 2021, I link appellate outcomes to judge-level workload and written reasoning. I instrument a presiding judge's caseload with the leave-one-out workload of other presiding judges in the same court and month. A doubling of appellate caseload increases the probability that the appellate court upholds the first-instance judgment by about 0.7 percentage points. Heavier caseloads also reduce legal citations and increase textual similarity between first-and second-instance reasoning. The results show that court congestion changes not only how quickly courts process disputes, but also how intensively appellate judges review lower-court decisions.

detail.abstract: The theory about reducing risk via portfolio diversification is so well-known that it has become financial conventional wisdom. Less well-known is the economic theory about partners along a supply chain and why partnering is more efficient than doing it all on your own. “How do firms choose trade partners?” is not an easy question to answer, but, as it turns out, is related to the theory of portfolio diversification. Understanding both of these theories is important to understanding how trade agreements impact market structure. 1 Firms interacting with each other along a supply chain–taking advantage of the benefits of specialization– reduces transactions costs. The profitability of value-added products is incentivized in these supply-chain relationships as trust along the chain increases.2 Contracts, especially those that are long established and with legally enforceable provisions, increase trust. With binding contracts, firms are able to meet the needs of other actors along the supply chain and tailor their products for specific needs thus increasing the value of the good. What happens when the contracts cannot be relied upon? Two possibilities emerge. When partnerships become unreliable, to mitigate risk firms either 1) go looking for other partners or 2) try to manage more of their supply chain internally.

detail.abstract: This paper studies regression discontinuity (RD) designs when the analysis sample is stratified on realized treatment status. Treatment-based sampling is common in program evaluation when treated units are rare, policy-relevant, or observed more intensively than nonparticipants. We show that the sharp RD treatment-effect estimand is preserved under such sampling, but the sampled density of the running variable may exhibit a mechanical discontinuity at the cutoff even when the population density is continuous. In fuzzy RD designs, the conventional local Wald ratio generally fails to identify the population complier effect at the cutoff. We derive an explicit principal-strata decomposition of the resulting bias and propose a reweighted fuzzy RD estimand that restores identification when the population treatment share is known, externally estimable, or treated as a sensitivity parameter. We develop weighted local-linear estimation, consistency, asymptotic bias and variance formulas, and a robust bias-corrected inference connection. Finally, we construct a reweighted density-continuity diagnostic that targets the population running-variable density rather than the distorted sample density and adapt local-polynomial density-discontinuity inference to this setting. Unlike standard IV settings, RD designs also rely on density-continuity diagnostics, so treatment-based sampling affects both the causal estimand in fuzzy RD and the diagnostic evidence used to validate the design.

detail.abstract: For this policy brief, I estimated the impact to Iowa’s State Gross Domestic Product (GDP), or “value added” for 60 industries encompassing agricultural production, processing or agricultural adjacent industries. Value added is the contribution to GDP, the difference between the sales output and the cost of intermediate inputs used to produce the output. I used an economic impact model maintained by the IMPLAN Group, LLC, Huntersville, NC (IMPLAN), which is often called an input-output (IO) production model. In this model, think of all industries in the economy as feeding inputs into each other to produce outputs that are then sold to consumers or sold to another industry along a supply chain. IO models make adjustments for imports and exports as well as government services while accounting for employment and taxes to the various industrial sectors in order to calculate how much additional value is added to the economy, as opposed to only examining sales receipts. IO models determine the linkages between and among different industries in the production of goods and services in the economy and can measure how dollars spent in one industry impact another. My definition of agricultural industries includes farm production (e.g., soybeans), processing of production into a new, manufactured product (e.g., soymeal, biodiesel), as well as the creation of products used in agricultural production (e.g., nitrogen fertilizer) and affiliated services like veterinary services. The specific industries as well as their general definitions are shown in table 1. I based my definitions on those provided by IMPLAN. Along with the IMPLAN industry codes, table 1 also provides the 6-digit North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes. Readers curious about the components of each industry can consult the documentation provided by these two establishments for more detail.1 One thing to notice is that some industries are quite broad. Ethanol, for example, is encompassed in the larger “other organic chemical” industry. Researchers are limited to the industries as defined by the NAICS and the government agencies that collect the data, and although future research could attempt to create specific industries in IO models, I do not attempt to do so here.

detail.abstract: Climate variability has substantially altered the livelihood of smallholder communities, especially in developing countries of Sub-Saharan African countries, where agriculture is mostly rainfed. In the pursuit of coping mechanisms, the most plausible avenues for farmers to increase their overall crop production include cropland expansion at the expanse of natural forest resources. Locally, climate variability perception within farming communities had not been sufficiently documented in developing countries. This is fundamentally due to data scarcity. Yet, such information is urgently needed to support the implementation of climate adaptation projects, both at sub-municipality and district levels. Here, using a semi-structure questionnaire administered to the farming community in Benin, a random sub-sample of 236 farmers was selected. To this survey data, historical precipitation data was complemented, spanning from 1990 to 2021, using selected farmers household locations during the growing season of year 2021, to compute the relative deviation from historical (30 years) seasonal trend. Descriptive statistics reveal that most farmers perceive the impact of climate variability, while a non-negligible proportion does not have access to weather information. There is a positive correlation between farmers who use organic fertilizer and the decrease in rainfall perception, corroborating that access to weather information would be helpful to smallholder farmers. Sensitivity to climate variability varies based on gender, indicating the necessity of agricultural extension services. This study demonstrates that smallholder farmers in Benin are negatively affected by rainfall shocks, which is a major contributor to migration and decrease in yields of dominant crops. A seasonal modeling framework is therefore necessary to further understand effects of climate variables on sub-national variations of crop production.

detail.abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) charging can significantly reshape peak electricity demand, yet most studies evaluate its impacts at either the bulk transmission or distribution level alone. This separation can obscure important tradeoffs between system-wide peak reduction and local load synchronization. This study evaluates the peak-demand impacts of light-duty battery electric vehicles across all 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia from 2026 to 2040 using a dual-metric framework that captures both bulk-system peak exposure, via a Peak Alignment Factor (PAF), and distribution-level load synchronization, via the traditional coincidence factor (CF). The results show that charging behavior is a larger determinant of peak demand than adoption itself. Under the base adoption scenario, unmanaged charging increases the non-coincident national peak by 59.9 GW by 2040 (59.2 GW coincident peak), while fully managed charging reduces this increase to 27.6 GW (28.5 GW coincident peak). Time-of-use (TOU) pricing minimizes it to 21.6 GW (21.4 GW coincident), but concentrates charging into the same overnight hours, producing a combined 189 GW non-coincident charging peak (97.8 GW coincident), compared with 72 GW under unmanaged charging. In six states, California, Colorado, New Jersey, Michigan, New York, and Hawaii, this synchronized midnight peak exceeds the existing evening peak and becomes a new system peak. Strategies that reduce transmission-level stress can raise distribution-level stress by concentrating charging into the same hours. By combining both metrics, the framework reveals a transmission-distribution tradeoff that single-metric approaches cannot detect. Among the strategies evaluated, only fully managed charging improves both at once. The results provide a nationwide basis for EV charging policy, infrastructure planning, and grid-reliability strategy.

detail.abstract:
Global trade finance continues to rely heavily on manual, paper-based processes, particularly in the management of Letters of Credit (LCs), resulting in inefficiencies, delays, high operational costs, and frequent documentation discrepancies. Despite the critical role of LCs in facilitating international trade, fragmented coordination among exporters, importers, banks, and logistics providers limits transparency and slows transaction execution. These challenges contribute to the growing global trade finance gap and disproportionately affect small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) seeking access to financing.

This white paper proposes a blockchain-based Smart Letter of Credit (Smart LC) Automation solution that leverages distributed ledger technology and smart contracts to digitize and automate trade finance workflows. By enabling real-time data sharing, immutable recordkeeping, automated compliance verification, and conditional payment execution, the proposed system reduces manual intervention, minimizes errors, and accelerates cross-border transactions. The solution is designed as a consortium blockchain network connecting all relevant stakeholders within a secure and transparent ecosystem.

The paper evaluates the business and strategic implications of Smart LC implementation through established blockchain business model frameworks, including the Magical Triangle, Blockchain Business Model Canvas, and Blockchain Business Model Taxonomy. Furthermore, it presents a practical integration approach, governance structure, and profitability assessment to demonstrate real-world feasibility and long-term value creation. The findings suggest that blockchain-enabled Smart LCs can significantly improve efficiency, reduce transaction costs, strengthen trust among participants, and increase accessibility to trade finance, particularly for SMEs. Ultimately, the proposed solution illustrates how blockchain technology can modernize trade finance infrastructure and support a more transparent, scalable, and inclusive global trading environment.

detail.abstract: This study examined how changes in exchange rates impacted the financial performance of Nigerian manufacturing businesses between 2012 and 2022, with a particular focus on Nestlé Nigeria Plc and Cadbury Nigeria Plc. The particular goals were to assess how return on equity (ROE) was impacted by the money supply (MSP), inflation rate (INFR), and real effective exchange rate (REER). The study used an ex post facto research approach, and multiple regression and pooled least squares were used to analyze the data. To give a more comprehensive contextual knowledge of the internal and external elements impacting business performance, a SWOT and PESTEL examination was also carried out. The empirical findings showed that the MSP has a positive but negligible impact on ROE (p = 0.4234), the INFR has a negative and insignificant impact on ROE (p = 0.1373), and REER has a positive but statistically insignificant influence on ROE (p = 0.2080). The explanatory variables together affect financial performance, as evidenced by the overall model's statistical significance (F-statistic p = 0.000001). The model's robustness was further supported by diagnostic tests, which revealed no significant problems with autocorrelation (p = 0.9741) or heteroskedasticity (p > 0.05). The study comes to the conclusion that, although their individual effects are minimal, macroeconomic factors as a whole have an impact on Nigerian manufacturing firms' performance. To improve sectoral performance, it recommends controlling inflation, stabilizing exchange rates, and expanding credit availability.

title: Nonlinearity and Harrod-Balassa-Samuelson Effects in Real Exchange Rates over the Past Two Centuries
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Nonlinearity and Harrod-Balassa-Samuelson Effects in Real Exchange Rates over the Past Two Centuries
detail.abstract: Lothian and Taylor (2008) found significant nonlinear mean reversion in the sterlingdollar and sterling-franc real exchange rates over 1820-2001, with a significant Harrod-Balassa-Samuelson (HBS) productivity effect for the former but not the latter. We extend their long-span data through 2022 and add three sterling bilateral real exchange rates over two centuries: Australia, Canada, and Japan. The original results survive the extensions, nonlinear adjustment is present across all five pairs, and HBS effects are significant in sterling-dollar and the three additional real exchange rates.

title: Constrained Stochasticity in Central Limit Order Books

detail.title: Constrained Stochasticity in Central Limit Order Books

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework for modeling Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) dynamics under the hypothesis of Constrained Stochasticity-the proposition that high-frequency price formation is simultaneously stochastic at the nanosecond level and structurally bounded by algorithmic liquidity architecture at meso-and macro-timescales. We introduce the Discretized Execution Validation Matrix (Φk), a tick-level operator that aggregates localized liquidity tensors, directional execution vectors, and volumetric mass via Hadamard composition. Embedding Φk within a three-state hidden Markov regime-switching model (Hamilton, 1989; Ang & Timmermann, 2012), we derive closed-form absorbing boundary conditions that govern leveraged wealth processes under each regime. Self-exciting order-flow dynamics are modeled via a discretized multivariate Hawkes point process (Hawkes, 1971; Bacry et al., 2015), permitting tractable estimation of endogenous liquidity feedback loops. Empirical validation is conducted on 24 months of Level-3 tick data from CME E-mini S&P 500 (ES) and E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) Futures (2022-2024), encompassing approximately 8.3 billion discrete order-book events. Walkforward out-of-sample testing produces annualized Sharpe ratios of 2.85 (Regime 1) and 1.42 (Regime 2), with full execution clamping activated during Regime 3 chaotic states. These results are statistically significant (p < 0.01) against a geometric Brownian motion null and survive Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons. All Section 5 results are presented as numerical illustrations based on live CME Globex Level-3 data; out-of-sample performance is not asserted as a guarantee of future returns. The framework offers actionable contributions to both the theoretical microstructure literature and the practical design of institutional execution engines.

By sustainable does not only mean sustainable act environmentally but also to build an organization that does not perish easily.
