title:
Tacit Bargains: Reciprocal Risk and Elite Access
A Theoretical Framework for Outsider Entry into Elite Institutional Networks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Tacit Bargains: Reciprocal Risk and Elite Access
A Theoretical Framework for Outsider Entry into Elite Institutional Networks
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the tacit bargain as a distinct theoretical concept, where an informal relationship forged through the deliberate sharing of vulnerable and destructive information, producing an irrevocable bond of mutual exposure that functions as one underexamined pathway of outsider entry into elite institutional networks. Existing elite theory documents how power is maintained once established but cannot account for how outsiders without conventional credentials achieve rapid incorporation. Existing secrecy theory explains what concealment does to relationships but does not ask how it enables the crossing from outside to inside. Existing trust theory identifies mutual vulnerability as a binding mechanism but confines this analysis to criminal or informal contexts. This paper argues that under specific scope conditions-where trust is scarce, stakes are high, formal vetting is limited, discretion is essential, and the outsider possesses something insiders cannot obtain through conventional channels, the tacit bargain enables outsiders to compress into a single deliberate act the trust that normally takes generations to accumulate. The framework is illustrated through two historically documented cases: Skull
and Bones, the Yale secret society whose membership has produced a disproportionate concentration of American political and intelligence elite, and the Rothschild banking network, whose founder achieved rapid incorporation into European aristocratic financial networks through deliberate vulnerability architecture. The paper concludes by examining the implications of this framework for how we understand meritocracy, democratic accountability, and the official
narratives elites construct about their own ascent.

title: Emergency Arbitration in India: Bridging the Statutory Vacuum Between Judicial Pragmatism and Legislative Reform
affiliations: Amity University Lucknow Campus and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Emergency Arbitration in India: Bridging the Statutory Vacuum Between Judicial Pragmatism and Legislative Reform
detail.abstract: Emergency arbitration has gained popularity in the last decade as an essential tool in international commercial arbitration. It helps to overcome a severe time gap, which cannot be sufficiently resolved in a regular course of litigation and common arbitral procedure by allowing parties to receive immediate interim relief by constituting an arbitral tribunal. It is also true that in India, the statute that regulated arbiter emergencies is not codified, judicially created, and it is unclear in its operationality. This paper explores the evolution of emergency arbitration in the Indian legal order, starting with the pre-statutory workaround context until the Supreme Court’s groundbreaking decision in Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC v Future Retail Ltd (2021) and the subsequent changes in legislation inspired by the decision. By relying on a comparative study of the most successful arbitral institutions, such as the SIAC, HKIAC, ICC, LCIA, SCC, and SAC, and placing the Indian experience in the context of international practice, this paper determines the structural weaknesses that still hinder the successful use and application of emergency awards in India. It ends with a series of specific reform proposals, comprising both model law and institutional rule changes, to bring emergency arbitration into the Indian statutory regime in a way that is consistent, binding, and competitive with existing arbitration-friendly jurisdictions.

title: Same-Gap Coupling and the (Im)possibility of Endogenous Distributive Cycles
affiliations: University of Brasília (UnB)

detail.title: Same-Gap Coupling and the (Im)possibility of Endogenous Distributive Cycles
detail.abstract: We ask which Harrodian-Cambridge accumulation-distribution closures can host endogenous distributive cycles, and resolve the question through one coordinate-free invariant: the sign of the Jacobian determinant at a gap-closing equilibrium. A rank-deficiency lemma shows that letting several slow variables read a common profit-rate gap-same-gap coupling-is, on its own, structurally insufficient for cycles; the degeneracy coincides with that of the standard longrun Kaleckian closure. A sign obstruction then establishes that repairing it through distribution alone leaves the equilibrium unstable. A minimal constructive model-Keynesian-stabilised accumulation with a profit-squeeze response-exhibits an isolated, locally stable equilibrium that loses stability through a Hopf bifurcation proved supercritical, the first Lyapunov coefficient being negative and robust. The Goodwin growth cycle is the limiting case. Cycles turn on feedback sign and channel, not dimension.

title: Environmental Regulation, Heterogeneous Firms, and Industry Performance
affiliations: Zhejiang University,  and School of Economics, Zhejiang University

detail.title: Environmental Regulation, Heterogeneous Firms, and Industry Performance
detail.abstract: How does environmental regulation affect firm behavior, industry performance, and welfare? We develop and estimate a structural model of production with endogenous emissions and costly abatement under heterogeneous regulation, using firm-level data that report net emissions but not abatement expenditures. The model recovers productivity, the shadow price of emissions, and the implicit output subsidy induced by intensity regulation. Applying the model to China's non-metallic mineral products industry over 1998-2007, we show that ignoring emissions conflates firm performance with compliance effort and disproportionately understates the productivity of less productive firms. Counterfactual analysis yields two main results. First, under emissions-intensity standards, welfare costs rise convexly as reduction targets tighten, with endogenous production responses accounting for up to 17% of the costs. Second, replacing intensity standards with an emissions trading system substantially lowers welfare costs of regulation, allowing emissions to fall by 44% without reducing total surplus.

title: Toward a General Theory of Sustainable Effective Demand under Rational Expectations
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Toward a General Theory of Sustainable Effective Demand under Rational Expectations
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a general conceptual framework for sustainable effective demand under rational expectations. The central claim is that policy-created demand should not be evaluated only by its immediate nominal spending effect. It should also be evaluated by whether temporary purchasing power can remain effective after rational expectations, money-value dilution, asset-price repricing, consumer-price adjustment, credit conditions, fiscal adjustment, occupational incentives, and social-cost burdens are incorporated into household and market behavior. 
The paper extends the Keynesian idea of effective demand by distinguishing temporary effective demand from sustainable effective demand. Temporary effective demand refers to immediate payment capacity generated by income, transfers, credit, or fiscal support. Sustainable effective demand refers to purchasing power that remains effective over time because it is supported by capital-accumulation capacity, stable expectation consistent real transfer earnings, and the ability to cross asset-entry barriers before prices and credit conditions adjust. 
The proposed framework reconciles Keynesian demand creation with rationalexpectations-based adjustment. Keynesian policy may raise demand in the short run. However, if policy undermines expectation consistency regarding future money value, inflation, taxation, fiscal adjustment, asset prices, or credit conditions, agents may reprice assets, adjust prices, alter saving behavior, and shift occupational choices before temporary income becomes durable purchasing power. Thus, the key policy problem is not merely how to create demand, but how to create demand without destroying the expectation structure that allows it to remain sustainable.
The paper develops several connected mechanisms. First, it formulates a fiscal expansion paradox: fiscal support may raise temporary effective demand while failing to create sustainable effective demand if high essential-consumption absorption prevents capital accumulation and if money-value dilution raises asset-entry barriers before households can accumulate capital. Second, it develops a wage and infrastructure-cost paradox: nominal wage increases can fail to increase real purchasing power when wage and non-wage infrastructure costs are cumulatively passed through production, logistics, distribution, finance, administration, taxation, compliance, and service chains. Third, it introduces occupational convexity as a human-capital consequence of expectation instability. If money value and asset value become unstable, expectation-adjusted real transfer earnings in ordinary occupations may become insufficient for life-cycle viability, causing labor supply to concentrate in high-income, high-rent, high-credit-access, or scalable occupations. This concentration weakens occupational convexity and reduces social welfare. 
The paper also proposes a Median-Anchored Ladder Dividend System as a policy mechanism for converting temporary fiscal support into capital-accumulation capacity. The system combines broad public asset inclusion, median settlement incentives, median convergence incentives, wage-growth incentives, and verified avoided social-cost dividends. It is designed to preserve survival protection while strengthening work incentives, middle-class formation, public asset claims, and expectation-consistent sustainable effective demand.  
The equations in this paper are conceptual and diagnostic rather than fully estimated econometric specifications. They are designed to make the theoretical mechanism explicit. Their coefficients, weights, functional forms, thresholds, and normalization rules should be calibrated according to national economic conditions, monetary regimes, fiscal capacity, asset-market structure, labor-market elasticity, credit systems, socialpolicy design, and institutional context. The framework should therefore be read as a general theoretical map for evaluating whether policy-created demand can remain sustainable under rational expectations.

title: Treasury Laws Amendment: Submission to Senate Economics Legislation Committee
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW), UNSW Business School

detail.title: Treasury Laws Amendment: Submission to Senate Economics Legislation Committee
detail.abstract: This submission makes several key policy proposals, which are grounded in the below extended analysis. The overarching finding is that the Treasury Laws Amendments are not fit for purpose and should be rejected outright. They risk reducing government revenue by setting bad incentives, create punitive provisions for people immigrating to or from Australia, vest unacceptable amounts of discretion in the treasurer, and set an undemocratic precedent. The laws will also deter value creation, including in improving or increasing housing supply. The laws should be rejected.

title: Agentic AI Payments and the Opportunities for MiCA-Compliant Stablecoins
affiliations: University San Raffaele Roma

detail.title: Agentic AI Payments and the Opportunities for MiCA-Compliant Stablecoins
detail.abstract: The e-commerce landscape is undergoing a structural transformation toward "agentic commerce", where autonomous AI agents execute complex transactions, driving a market projected to reach between $3 trillion and $5 trillion by 2030. This monumental shift is fundamentally incompatible with the traditional financial system, which is designed for human consumers and cannot handle the high volume of near-instant, fractions-of-a-cent microtransactions required for machine-to-machine payments. This paper argues that stablecoins are the critical infrastructure for the agentic economy, providing the requisite predictable value, 24/7 liquidity, and low-cost settlement that volatile cryptocurrencies and slow legacy fiat rails cannot. Crucially, the stablecoin market poised to win this multi-trillion-dollar frontier is one built on regulatory trust. While many stablecoins suffer from opaque reserves and regulatory uncertainty, MiCA-compliant stablecoins possess a competitive edge. Europe's stringent MiCA Regulation requires 1:1 backing by safeguarded, bankruptcy-remote fiat reserves in Tier-1 EU banks, a "compliance-by-design" approach that provides the enterprise-grade assurance large multinational corporations require. Furthermore, MiCA's integration with AMLA and Verification of Payee standards ensures auditable, risk-managed boundaries for autonomous workflows. This unique combination of frictionless payment capabilities and robust European regulatory oversight positions MiCA-compliant stablecoins to become the foundational layer and market leader for automated e-commerce value transfer.

title: CAIRN: Cost-Aware Information Routing for Underwriting

detail.title: CAIRN: Cost-Aware Information Routing for Underwriting
detail.abstract: A lending decision is a sequence of purchases of information. Each external source-a business register, a credit bureau, an open-banking feed, an asset valuation-carries a price and buys a quantum of certainty about a borrower. Production engines acquire a fixed waterfall of these sources for every applicant. We introduce CAIRN (Cost-Aware Information Routing for uNderwriting), an agentic engine that instead treats each acquisition as a Pandora's box in the sense of Weitzman and opens the next box only while its value of information exceeds its cost. The central contribution is a dual-currency cost: every source is priced as a vendor fee plus the monetised cost of the large-language-model tokens burned to ingest and reason over it. We cast the full intake-to-settlement workflow as a partially observable Markov decision process whose belief state is coupled to IFRS 9 PD, LGD, EAD and SICR models, so the value of information is expressed in expected-loss pounds and scales with exposure. Across a synthetic UK loan-book of 1,200 applications under realistic vendor fees, CAIRN reduces cost per decision by 38.7% (from £33.54 to £20.57) while achieving lower regret against a perfect-information oracle-of order £1.3m a year at one hundred thousand applications. We are deliberately honest about where the saving arises: at current vendor pricing it is driven by fee avoidance and the token term is second-order, yet the token term is the correct general model, is the entire cost of nominally free open-data sources and becomes first-order as reasoning models grow more token-hungry. The engine ring-fences mandatory compliance checks, audits every decision to the individual acquisition event, and attaches a plain-English rationale.

title: The Transmission Efficiency of Net Investment Is Decreasing in the Replacement Burden

detail.title: The Transmission Efficiency of Net Investment Is Decreasing in the Replacement Burden
detail.abstract: Standard analyses of investment and growth estimate a single transmission elasticity-one number summarizing how net investment maps into output growth. We show this number is not a constant but a function of the replacement burden 𝛿 = CFC/VA, and that the function declines: a unit of net investment generates progressively less output growth as 𝛿 rises. We estimate the shape of this function-the gradient of the transmission coefficient across the 𝛿 distribution-on a primary country specification whose splitter and regressor carry no value added (𝛿 𝐾 = CFC/𝐾, net investment on the capital stock), so output enters only the outcome. Transmission attenuates by roughly 25-33% through the bulk of the distribution, significant under wild-cluster-bootstrap inference. A fully decoupled specification in which the splitter and regressor share no denominator at all yields the same monotone decline, and a placebo calibration shows the conventional outputdenominator specification could reproduce the observed gradient only under transitory outputmeasurement noise an order of magnitude larger than national accounts admit. The same decline appears at three independent levels of aggregation-a 31-country OECD panel, a 9,019-observation OECD STAN industry panel, and a 251,130 firm-year Compustat panel-whose fixed-effects structures share nothing and whose observation counts differ by more than two orders of magnitude.

title: Minimum Wages and the Informality Constraint
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Minimum Wages and the Informality Constraint

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: How does informality shape the impact of minimum wage policy? We study this question using evidence from Mexico’s 145% real increase in the minimum wage since 2016, together with a general equilibrium model featuring endogenous informality and household heterogeneity. Reduced-form estimates of the implemented increases indicate limited effects on employment and formalization, alongside modest wage gains at the bottom of the formal wage distribution that arguably reflect incomplete enforcement. The calibrated model reproduces these patterns but predicts that, under full enforcement, higher wage floors generate nonlinear effects: the share of firms reallocating toward informality rises sharply, lowering productivity and aggregate welfare. These losses fall disproportionately on low-skill households, who bear the brunt of the reduction in transfers caused by lower tax revenue yet, as predominantly informal workers, gain little directly from the minimum wage. The minimum wage’s effectiveness as a redistributive tool is therefore limited.

title: The (Many) Consequences of the Housing Affordability Problem in the EU
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The (Many) Consequences of the Housing Affordability Problem in the EU

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Housing affordability is high on the economic, social, and political agenda in Europe. While the economic literature has mostly analyzed the drivers of housing unaffordability, this paper focuses on its consequences, quantifying, at the EU level, its impact on individuals’ well-being as well as its economic and demographic impact. We find that the impact of an increase in housing cost burden is large on housing adequacy as well as on poverty and health. It is somewhat smaller on fertility and labor force participation.

title: Who Exports, Diversifies, and Upgrades in the Philippines? A Firm-level Analysis
affiliations: De La Salle University, United Nations University (UNU-MERIT) and Independent

detail.title: Who Exports, Diversifies, and Upgrades in the Philippines? A Firm-level Analysis
detail.abstract: We assemble a firm-level panel dataset that spans the years 2012-2021 with 52,795 observations, to examine which Philippine firms export, diversify, and upgrade, and whether firms that engage in these activities grow faster. Employing regression tree analysis, and endogenous switching to correct for selection bias, we find that: (i) foreign ownership and size are the strongest predictors of exporting and diversifying but are weak predictors of product upgrading. Exporters and diversifiers are highly concentrated in very large, foreign firms; (ii) exporting positively affects employment and sales growth for exporters, but it is negatively associated with labor productivity growth. For non-exporters, we do not find any statistically significant effects; (iii) the introduction of new products into a firm's export portfolio significantly enhances employment growth, sales, and labor productivity growth. If non-diversifying firms had diversified, they would have experienced productivity declines; (iv) introducing new products that are more complex than those existing in a firm's export portfolio positively impacts labor productivity growth. The productivity benefits of upgrading appear to extend beyond firms that actually upgrade, suggesting that the returns to upgrading are uniform across firms. These findings highlight the importance of not just participating in trade, but of upgrading and diversifying as key mechanisms through which trade contributes to firm growth.

title: Maintaining Financial Sector Integrity: Integrating Sustainable Finance into Financial Regulation
affiliations: University of Indonesia (UI), Other Firms, Universitas Negeri Semarang and Bank

detail.title: Maintaining Financial Sector Integrity: Integrating Sustainable Finance into Financial Regulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Private and Commercial Law, volume 10, issue 1, 2026[10.15294/jpcl.v10i1.45061]

detail.abstract: This article invetigates whether the integration of sustainable finance into the Indonesian financial regulatory framework aligns with established principles of financial regulation and whether such integration strengthens or potentially undermines financial sector integrity. This study assesses Indonesia's sustainable finance framework through a normative legal research approach. The study applies indicators derived from the principles of financial regulation, namely prudential risk integration, transparency and disclosure reliability, market integrity, supervisory effectiveness, and enforceability of sustainability-related obligations. Sustainable finance aims to incorporate environmental and social risks, especially those related to climate, into financial decision-making, but its regulatory implementation prompts significant inquiries about prudence, transparency, market integrity, and public confidence. The research indicates that Indonesia's sustainable finance governance faces three critical challenges: legitimacy risks stemming from vague green product classifications that enable greenwashing and erode trust, reputational risks caused by a lack of rigorous verification and mispricing concerns. Additional shortcomings include weak verification mechanisms for sustainability claims and the risk of symbolic compliance without substantive integration into prudential supervision. The research further finds that sustainable finance has a dual nature: when firmly rooted in legal authority, incorporated into prudential oversight, backed by uniform disclosure frameworks, and upheld through reliable supervisory systems, it boosts systemic resilience and strengthens regulatory legitimacy. On the other hand, disjointed execution, lax verification criteria, symbolic compliance, and inadequate enforcement can lead to greenwashing, regulatory arbitrage, mispricing, and reputational spillover, thereby threatening reputation of financial sector. The research finds that the effectiveness of sustainable finance in Indonesia relies on careful regulatory frameworks, strong institutional capabilities, and efficient enforcement to maintain the integrity of the financial sector.

detail.abstract: Inequality in the United States continues to rise sharply and academics are increasingly paying attention to the relationship between the law and the most vulnerable, making poverty law both important and timely. This Article is an architectural map of poverty law that sets out to define the field for future scholarly engagement. It attempts to answer three related questions: what has the government done to help poor people, what is poverty law, and how have poverty policies and scholarship changed over time? The field of poverty law has been around since the War on Poverty, yet, surprisingly, there is relatively little written about the nature of the field. This makes it difficult for those doing work at the periphery of antipoverty policy or new to poverty law to know the contours and history of the field. This Article fills this gap, showing the arc of antipoverty policies and poverty law scholarship from its New Deal origins and heights of influence during the War on Poverty to the conservative backlash that followed and fragmented resurgence of the field today.

title: Financial Wellbeing and Employment in the First Year of a Choice-Based Guaranteed Income Model
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - Brown School, Clark Atlanta University, Appalachian State University, Clark Atlanta University, Washington University in St. Louis, Morehouse School of Medicine, Clark Atlanta University,  and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Financial Wellbeing and Employment in the First Year of a Choice-Based Guaranteed Income Model

declarations.ethicsApproval: Appalachian State University Protocol IRB-22-0037
declarations.funderStatement: The authors would further like to express their gratitude to the Georgia Resilience and Opportunity Fund and GiveDirectly for their partnership on this project.

detail.abstract:
Guaranteed income (GI) programs have expanded rapidly in the United States over the past decade. However, gaps remain in the evidence base regarding program design features that support participant self-determination and longer-term financial stability. This paper presents Year One findings from In Her Hands Phase Two, a 36-month guaranteed income program serving 275 low-income women in historically Black neighborhoods on Atlanta's Westside. Phase Two is distinguished by two design features not previously tested at scale in U.S. GI research: a transfer amount ($36,000 total per recipient) and duration substantially larger than most prior pilots, and a participant choice model that allows recipients to select their own disbursement structure (either an $8,000 lump sum plus $800 per month for the remaining 35 months, or $1,000 per month for 36 months). Using a mixed-methods convergent design that integrates baseline application data, a 12-month follow-up survey (n = 135 treatment, n = 166 control), and two waves of qualitative interviews, we examine financial well-being and employment outcomes after the program’s first year.

At Year One, treatment participants were significantly less likely to report that covering monthly expenses was very difficult (33.0% vs. 49.3%, p < .01), less likely to report utility payment shortfalls (61.8% vs. 74.8%, p < .05), more likely to have any emergency savings (17.8% vs. 7.6%, p < .05), and more likely to have $500 or more in savings (16.8% vs. 4.5%, p < .05). These effects were robust to covariate adjustment and were concentrated among parents and participants with monthly incomes above $1,000. No significant treatment effects on debt or high-cost financial service use were observed, though results were directionally positive. Employment findings provided no evidence of labor market withdrawal: full-time employment rates and weekly hours worked among employed participants were statistically indistinguishable across groups.

Sixty-nine percent of treatment participants selected the lump-sum option. No demographic characteristic significantly predicted the choice of payment structure. At Year One, lump-sum and monthly recipients showed comparable financial well-being outcomes. Qualitative data provided additional context, documenting the individualized reasoning behind payment structure choices and describing GI as creating practical breathing room.

title: Cyber Espionage, Epistemic Asymmetry, And the Reorientation of International Law
affiliations: Carleton University

detail.title: Cyber Espionage, Epistemic Asymmetry, And the Reorientation of International Law
detail.abstract:
This article reframes cyber espionage as epistemic coercion: the anticipatory impairment of a state's capacity to know, reason, and decide on its own terms. Using Timor-Leste v. Australia as a point of departure, it shows that the decisive injury in contemporary operations is not destruction or territorial violation, but the conditioning of judgment through persistent access, surveillance, modeling, and infrastructural dependence. The result is cognitive displacement, where sovereign choices appear autonomous yet carry the imprint of external informational design.

Existing doctrines of sovereignty, non-intervention, due diligence, attribution, and human rights remain calibrated to visible and episodic harms, and therefore fail to register structural and ambient interference. This article advances two moves. First, it reconceives sovereignty as epistemic autonomy, a baseline of cognitive independence required for equal participation in law. Second, it articulates epistemic asymmetry as a legally cognizable mode of domination. To operationalize these claims, it proposes a Cognitive Displacement Test comprising three cumulative indicators: prolonged asymmetrical access to deliberative systems; observable substitution of legal reasoning through anticipatory mechanisms; and demonstrable constraint in a state’s legal posture.

The article sketches doctrinal adjustments and institutional pathways, and argues for jurisgenerative resistance and an epistemic constitutionalism that ties legal authority to transparent, verifiable knowledge practices.

title: Generations in Transition: Negotiating Transnational Identity and Gross National Happiness Among Bhutanese Youth in Perth
affiliations: and

detail.title: Generations in Transition: Negotiating Transnational Identity and Gross National Happiness Among Bhutanese Youth in Perth
detail.abstract:
Bhutan is undergoing significant demographic and social transition as growing numbers of young people pursue education, employment and life opportunities beyond national borders. While youth out-migration is often framed in Bhutanese public discourse as a threat to cultural continuity and national development, far less attention has been paid to how young Bhutanese themselves experience mobility and negotiate identity, belonging

and wellbeing outside Bhutan. This paper addresses this gap by examining how Bhutanese youth living in Perth, Western Australia, construct transnational identities in relation to the philosophy of Gross National Happiness (GNH). Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 Bhutanese youth aged 18–25, the study adopts a qualitative, interpretive approach to explore everyday understandings of being Bhutanese abroad, meanings of home and belonging, and evolving notions of happiness and wellbeing. The findings reveal that youth mobility does not signal detachment from Bhutan or rejection of GNH. Instead, young people actively negotiate inherited values and new social realities, producing hybrid identities shaped by family obligations, transnational aspirations, and lived experiences across borders. GNH emerges not as a fixed policy framework, but as a moral repertoire that travels with people and is selectively adapted in mobile contexts.

title: Artificial Intelligence: Bane or Boon? Socio-economic Challenges of the Future
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence: Bane or Boon? Socio-economic Challenges of the Future
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming industries, economies, and daily life by improving efficiency, innovation, and productivity. However, its rapid growth also raises concerns about job displacement, economic inequality, privacy, surveillance, and ethical challenges. This paper explores the benefits and risks of AI, its impact on society and global power structures, and the socio-economic issues humanity may face in the future. It concludes that responsible governance, ethical regulations, and education reforms are essential to ensure that AI serves as a tool for human progress rather than a source of harm.

title: Controlling Market Power in ASEAN: A Comparative Institutional Law and Economics Analysis of the Intellectual Property-Competition Law Interface

detail.title: Controlling Market Power in ASEAN: A Comparative Institutional Law and Economics Analysis of the Intellectual Property-Competition Law Interface

contentType.other: Submitted to Editors of Oxford Handbook

publicationDetails.detailsText: submitted to Editors of Oxford Handbook

detail.abstract:
Much of the scholarship concerning the intellectual property–competition law interface remains heavily doctrinal. Analysis commonly focuses upon compulsory licensing, refusals to deal, standard-essential patents (SEPs), patent settlements, technology transfer agreements and platform access obligations. Such work has generated valuable insights. However, it frequently assumes institutional environments like those of advanced jurisdictions, particularly those of the United States and the European Union.

This chapter argues that the interaction between intellectual property and competition law cannot be understood adequately through doctrinal analysis alone. The appropriate balance between intellectual property protection and competition law intervention depends critically upon institutional capacity, development strategy, market structure and political economy. Legal rules do not operate in the abstract. Their economic significance depends upon the institutions that interpret, administer and enforce them.

detail.abstract: Nowcasting models based on machine learning (ML) algorithms deliver a noteworthy advantage for decision-making in the public and private sectors due to their flexibility and ability to handle large amounts of data. This article introduces real-time forecasting models for the monthly Peruvian GDP growth rate. These models merge structured macroeconomic indicators with high-frequency unstructured sentiment variables. The analysis spans January 2007 to May 2023, encompassing a set of 91 leading economic indicators. Six ML algorithms were evaluated to identify the most effective predictors for each model. The findings underscore the remarkable capability of ML models to yield more precise and foresighted predictions compared to conventional time series models. Notably, the gradient boosting machine, LASSO, and elastic net models emerged as standout performers, achieving a reduction in prediction errors of 20% to 25% compared to autoregression and various specifications of dynamic factor model. These results could be influenced by the analysis period, which includes crisis events featuring high uncertainty, where ML models with unstructured data improve significance.

title: A Constitutional Critique of University Admission Quotas in Nigeria

detail.title: A Constitutional Critique of University Admission Quotas in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Nigeria admits students into its federal universities under a quota regime that reserves forty-five per cent of places for merit, thirty-five per cent for candidates from the institution's catchment area, and twenty per cent for candidates from states classified as educationally less developed. The regime was born of a legitimate and even noble constitutional purpose: the federal character principle and the post-civil-war project of national integration. This paper argues that the regime, as presently operated, has drifted from that purpose into a standing source of concrete injustice; that it sits in an unresolved and largely unexamined tension with the right to freedom from discrimination; and that the Supreme Court, in Badejo v. Federal Minister of Education, effectively sealed the courthouse door against the candidates the regime burdens, not by vindicating the policy on its merits but by declining to reach the merits at all. Drawing on the non-justiciability architecture of section 6(6)(c) and the Chapter II jurisprudence, the paper contends that the constitutional silence is neither inevitable nor honourable. It maps a route the courts and the legislature have not yet taken, through the domesticated African Charter and the legislative power to render directive principles justiciable and proposes a recalibration that retains the integrative aim while ending the arbitrariness.

Background: Current guidelines recommend deferring percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for functionally non-ischemic (fractional flow reserve [FFR] >0.80) intermediate coronary lesions. However, the long-term safety of this deferral strategy remains particularly uncertain in lesions harboring high-risk anatomical features.

Methods: In this retrospective cohort study, we enrolled 410 patients with chronic coronary syndrome who had at least one angiographically intermediate lesion (50-89% diameter stenosis). All qualifying lesions were retrospectively confirmed to be functionally nonischemic by angiographyderived fractional flow reserve (FFR > 0.80), yielding a total of 550 lesions for analysis. Management strategy (PCI vs. deferral) was determined by realworld clinical practice. The primary endpoint was the vesseloriented composite endpoint (VOCE), comprising vesselspecific myocardial infarction and ischemiadriven target vessel revascularization.

Results: Over a median follow-up of 9 years, the primary outcome occurred in 13.3% of deferred lesions and 9.1% of PCItreated lesions (HR 1.575, 95% CI 0.946 - 2.639, P=0.081). The safety of deferral varied substantially according to the burden of highrisk anatomical features (defined as stenosis ≥70%, multivessel disease, or LAD involvement). Among lesions with 0 or 1 of these highrisk features, VOCE rates were similar between the deferral and PCI groups (adjusted HR 0.629, 95% CI 0.216 - 1.930, P=0.397). In contrast, deferral of lesions with ≥2 highrisk features was associated with a significantly elevated longterm risk of VOCE at both 5 years (22.4% vs. 7.2%; adjusted HR 3.155, 95% CI 1.634 - 6.173, P=0.0006) and 9 years (28.2% vs. 9.4%; adjusted HR 3.367, 95% CI 1.869 - 6.098, P<0.0001).

Conclusions and Relevance: Uniform deferral of PCI for functionally nonischemic lesions may not be appropriate across all anatomical subsets. Our findings suggest that anatomical risk stratification can identify patients who are unlikely to benefit from conservative management, while reinforcing the safety of deferral in lowerrisk lesions. Integrating both functional and anatomical assessment may refine clinical decisionmaking and surveillance strategies.

​Background: Screening for colorectal cancer has led to large increases in the detection of large non-pedunculated rectal polyps. Local en bloc removal is increasingly seen as the optimal approach and can be performed by surgical or endoscopic local excision, via transanal minimal invasive surgery (TAMIS) or endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) respectively. We hypothesised that ESD would have a non-inferior recurrence rate with less serious adverse events and lower costs than TAMIS. 

Methods: We performed a multicentre randomised controlled non-inferiority trial in 23 hospitals in the Netherlands. Adult patients with a non-pedunculated rectal polyp larger than two centimetres without features of deep submucosal invasion, were eligible for inclusion. Patients were randomised 1:1 to receive TAMIS or ESD, stratified for the distance from the dentate line and lesion size. The primary outcome was the intention-to-treat recurrence rate at 12 months. The non-inferiority margin was six percent. Netherlands Trial Register, NL7083. 

Findings: 198 patients were recruited between Jan 1, 2019, and Jan 1, 2023. 98 (57 males) were assigned to TAMIS and 100 (60 males) to ESD. For the primary outcome all randomised patients were analysed. There were six recurrences in the TAMIS arm and none in the ESD arm. The difference in recurrence rate was –6·3% in favour of ESD (95% CI [ –11·2; –1·4]). ESD cost €2,636 (95% CI [2,446; 2,826]) and TAMIS €3,340 (95% CI [3,068; 3611]. There were no treatment related deaths and no significant differences in adverse events. 

Interpretation: ESD should be the treatment of choice for large non-pedunculated rectal polyps.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first global empirical evidence on the trade effects of losing shared regional trade agreement (RTA) coverage. Moving beyond single RTA exit cases, I study worldwide bilateral trade flows from 1980 to 2016 and estimate the effect of de-coverage using a structural gravity model together with a heterogeneity-robust staggered difference-in-differences design. I find that de-coverage reduces bilateral trade by about 37% on average, a magnitude similar to the gains from RTA formation. A key contrast with the RTA entry literature is its dynamics: while trade gains from RTA formation build up gradually over time, the adjustment to de-coverage is front-loaded. Heterogeneity analysis shows larger losses for dyads with longer prior RTA histories, geographically distant partners, and country pairs with asymmetric income levels. Product-level estimates show declines concentrated in intermediate and consumption goods.

detail.title: Domain-adaptive mixture-of-experts for cross-dataset lithium-Ion battery SOH prediction via adaptive strategy selection
detail.abstract: Accurate cross-dataset state of health prediction for lithium-ion batteries remains challenging due to distribution shifts arising from diverse cathode chemistries, operating temperatures, and charge-discharge protocols across heterogeneous battery fleets. This study proposes a Domain-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts framework that automatically selects the optimal domain adaptation strategy for each target domain through a lightweight linear gating network comprising merely 32 learnable parameters. The framework integrates a shared Transformer-based backbone with four adaptation strategies spanning the full spectrum of target-domain information utilization, namely Zero-shot transfer, Test-Time Adaptation, Fine-Tuning, and Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning. Comprehensive evaluation on 564 battery cells from seven publicly available datasets under Leave-One-Domain-Out Cross Validation protocol demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves an average coefficient of determination of 0.864 with perfect oracle strategy alignment under full domain training and maintains competitive generalization at average [[EQUATION]] of 0.795 when each target domain is held out during gating network training. Hard argmax selection consistently outperforms weighted fusion across all seven domains with an average margin of +0.027 in [[EQUATION]], confirming that the four adaptation strategies compete rather than cooperate in this application context. Feature ablation analysis identifies sample count as the dominant determinant of strategy selection with performance degradation of [[EQUATION]] upon removal, followed by degradation slope and knee-point ratio as secondary signals. The proposed framework provides a practically deployable solution for battery management systems operating across heterogeneous fleets with minimal computational overhead and strong cross-dataset generalization capability.

detail.title: Fire sales beyond banks: Fiscal news, leveraged non-bank investors, and sovereign bond-market stress
detail.abstract: This paper studies a general mechanism through which fiscal news can triggersovereign bond-market stress: when leveraged non-bank investors hold long-durationsovereign debt subject to collateral constraints, the same repricing of durationrisk that raises yields can also force asset sales and generate a self-reinforcingliquidity premium. We develop a small open economy New Keynesian model thatcombines two distinct intermediation frictions in the long-bond market. Patientarbitrageurs price duration risk, so that net duration supply moves the termpremium; constrained dealers price the immediacy of forced-sale flows, so thatinventory absorption moves a separate liquidity premium. Leveraged non-bankinvestors face an occasionally binding collateral constraint: unfunded fiscal newsraises expected deficits, public debt, and duration-risk supply, loweringlong-bond prices, tightening collateral conditions, and, once inherited pressurecrosses a threshold, triggering forced sales that dealers absorb only at a cost.The model separates four components of bond-market stress: expectations-hypothesisrepricing, a term/duration premium, a fiscal credibility/default premium, and amarket-functioning liquidity premium. We use the 2022 UK gilt-market crisis, inwhich liability-driven investment (LDI) funds were forced to sell gilts into afalling market, as the motivating laboratory for the calibration. In the baselinecalibration, the unfunded fiscal-news shock activates the collateral constraint,raises the peak long yield by about 155 basis points, generates a liquiditypremium of about 60 basis points, and lowers output by about 0.8 percent at thetrough. A high-buffer counterfactual that keeps the fiscal shock unchanged butprevents the constraint from binding reduces the peak long-yield response by about53 basis points and the output loss by about 0.34 percentage points. A central-bankmarket-functioning backstop sharply compresses the liquidity premium and forcedsales while leaving the fiscal-risk and term-premium components essentiallyunchanged. A key result is that financial amplification and real transmission arepartial substitutes: when private demand is less exposed to long rates, the samefire-sale loop shows up mainly in yields, whereas stronger long-rate exposureabsorbs part of the shock as a demand contraction. The mechanism is not specificto the UK episode; it applies wherever leveraged non-bank investors hold safelong-duration assets against binding collateral.

detail.title: Income vs. Asset Tests in the Safety Net: Impacts on Access, Targeting, and Costs in SNAP
detail.abstract: Means-tested programs worldwide screen applicants on both income and assets, yet little is known about the comparative effects of relaxing each screen. We provide the first within-program comparison, exploiting the staggered adoption of Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility in SNAP, under which some U.S. states relaxed only the asset test while others also raised the gross income threshold. Using a stacked difference-indifferences design, we find that raising the income threshold increased both eligibility and enrollment by roughly twice as much as relaxing the asset test, with roughly half of the enrollment response coming from inframarginal households who were previously eligible but not enrolled. At the same time, newly eligible households under income expansion were more disadvantaged than those under asset relaxation, and raising the income threshold brought in enrollees who were on some dimensions needier than baseline enrollees. For benefit amounts, average benefits per enrollee remained similar across the two expansions despite the income expansion making many low-benefit households newly eligible, as few of these households actually enrolled. Simulations further suggest that incorporating asset information into the benefit formula could substantially improve the targeting of benefit dollars toward the most disadvantaged households.

detail.abstract: The spectator task elicits third parties’ inequality acceptance, allowing researchers to estimate population distributions of fairness-preference types. In its within-subject form, spectators make two subsequent choices in situations involving merit- and luck-based inequalities with randomized order. We document a carry-over effect: redistribution is lower in the second choice, and inferred fairness-type distributions vary with choice order. We cannot determine whether this pattern is driven by a psychological mechanism active during repeated choices or a contrast between inequality causes. Either interpretation implies a violation of causal transience and calls for caution when using this design.

detail.title: Environmental impoverishment, ecological distribution conflicts and multi-dimensional poverty
detail.abstract: The word “development” is synonymous to economic growth in the UN Sustainable Development Goal 8. We know however that after Amartya Sen’s 1999 book “Development as Freedom”, development did not mean increased income per capita but a decrease in poverty and a wide exercising of capabilities and of freedom of choice. How was the measurement of the decrease in poverty to be operationalized? The answer was the MDP index (multidimensional poverty index), and previously also the HDI (human development index), where income per capita is one of three factors. In this article, we highlight the multi-criteria approach of the MDP Index that captures the multiple deprivations poor people experience with respect not so much to income as to health, education, and living standards. We notice however the lack of indicators of local and global environmental impoverishment in the MDP Index. In contrast, such dimensions are extremely visible in the Ecological Distribution Conflicts (EDC) collected in the EJAtlas. People get impoverished by land and water grabbing, climate change, biocultural loss, the displacements caused by economic growth and the concomitant changes in the social metabolism. The poor complain and display different valuation languages. Sometimes they coalesce in movements for environmental justice against the socio-ecological deprivations they suffer. This paper therefore brings together ecological economics, political ecology and development economics emphasizing the clash between economic growth and the preservation and enhancement of the social and natural environment.

title: Does conservation agriculture increase resilience to adverse weather? Field-level evidence
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU), College of Food, Agricultural & Environmental Science, Agricultural, Environmental & Development Economics, Students, Kansas State University - Department of Agricultural Economics and Kansas State University

detail.title: Does conservation agriculture increase resilience to adverse weather? Field-level evidence
detail.abstract: Agricultural conservation practices have the potential to increase crops' resilience to extreme weather shocks, but there is limited evidence of these benefits outside of research trials or case studies. In this study, we explore whether farm-level outcomes from the Federal crop insurance program (FCIP) can advance understanding of the degree to which common conservation practices increase resilience. The FCIP is a key part of crop farms' risk management strategies and nearly all acreage of major crops is currently enrolled. We observe farm-level production practices, insurance use, and insurance payouts in the USDA's Agricultural Resource Management Survey (ARMS), a multi-year, nationally representative field- and farm-level survey of major field crops. We first consider evidence for the interdependence of crop insurance participation and conservation practice adoption. We find that crop insurance use has a varied relationship with conservation practices, which then, in turn, influence insurance indemnity outcomes in some cases. Our primary estimating equations test whether farms using specific tillage practices or cover crops have lower likelihoods and amounts of crop insurance indemnity payouts after exposure to atypical growing-season weather. For practices that are unrelated or positively related to crop insurance choices, we find evidence of lower crop insurance payouts in years with excess rainfall. Conservation practices may increase resilience to weather shocks, but analysis of policy outcomes to assess this relationship should account for how risk management and conservation choices may be jointly determined.

title: Beyond Prediction: A Geometric Diagnostic Framework for Similarity-Adjusted Benefit Transfer
affiliations: Department of Agriculture, Food and Environment

detail.title: Beyond Prediction: A Geometric Diagnostic Framework for Similarity-Adjusted Benefit Transfer
detail.abstract: Benefit transfer accuracy depends critically on the similarity between study and policy sites, yet this condition is rarely assessed formally. This paper introduces the Similarity-Adjusted Benefit Transfer (SABT) framework, which reconceptualises similarity as the central criterion underlying the empirical defensibility of benefit transfer. SABT has a dual structure: the first component is a diagnostic framework that determines ex ante whether the conditions for reliable transfer are satisfied; the second is a transfer mechanism — a similarity-weighted average of donor values, analogous to the sales comparison approach in real estate appraisal. In data-sparse contexts, the diagnostic component may be more valuable than the transfer component itself, because it can reveal that no weighted-average method will outperform the simple mean. Three diagnostic instruments are developed: convex-hull analysis in Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-reduced space, the Effective Number of Donors (END) metric based on the inverse Herfindahl–Hirschman index of the weight vector, and a three-step transferability screening protocol. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that pool diversity — not pool size — drives SABT’s discriminatory power. These diagnostics are method-agnostic: they constitute a reliability layer applicable on top of meta-analytic regression, locally weighted estimation, and machine-learning approaches. The framework is tested on a dataset of 8 Mediterranean wetland sites — a deliberately small pool representing the conditions for which SABT is designed, where meta-regression is infeasible and practitioners must rely on unit-value transfer. Results confirm that transfer accuracy is governed by geometric position in attribute space rather than by weighting kernel, distance metric, or attribute configuration.

title: Sensory valuation of nature: Stated preferences based on visual and olfactory impressions

detail.title: Sensory valuation of nature: Stated preferences based on visual and olfactory impressions
detail.abstract: Using visualization in stated preference studies has become a widespread practice while other stimuli, despite their relevance in explaining people’s valuation of nature, are rarely used. In our experiment in the field, we tested whether providing olfactory stimuli affects stated preferences compared to only showing visual stimuli. We experimentally varied the visual and olfactory states of beach quality to systematically test whether combining these stimuli could reduce the hypothetical bias in stated preference elicitation and lead to greater evaluability. To test the effect of the setting, we ran the experiment in a field setting, i.e. at the beach, and outside the field setting. While challenging to implement in real-world settings, our empirical results demonstrate that omitting stimuli relevant to a particular environmental setting is likely to introduce bias into the results of stated preference studies, with implications for their elicitation.

title: Paths of Risk: Carbon Transmission Through Supply Chain Networks and the Cost of Equity Capital
affiliations: University of Oxford, Power Management Institute India and University of Oxford

detail.title: Paths of Risk: Carbon Transmission Through Supply Chain Networks and the Cost of Equity Capital
detail.abstract: This study investigates the transmission of carbon risk through supply chain networks and its impact on a firm’s implied cost of equity capital (ICOE). Using dyadic firm-level data, we document that carbon risk transmitted from customers is priced into the focal firm's implied cost of equity, while supplier carbon risk yields no such effect, suggesting a directional asymmetry in climate risk transmission along the supply chain. We identify cash flow volatility as a key transmission channel, whereby customer carbon risk increases uncertainty in the focal firm’s cash flows, leading investors to demand a higher risk premium. Higher network criticality of customers, more central role in supply chain networks and the focal firm’s sales structure, amplifies the pricing of carbon risk from customers, while a more gradual policy commitment attenuates this impact. Sectoral heterogeneity analysis further reveals that the effect of carbon risk transmitted from customers within the power sector supply chain is three times higher than the baseline estimates. Our findings suggest that policymakers should closely monitor the interdependence of carbon risk across value chains, with particular attention to high-emission sectors such as the power sector supply chain.

title: Why Gold, Now? Four Structural Developments That Supersede the Conventional Sizing Framework

detail.title: Why Gold, Now? Four Structural Developments That Supersede the Conventional Sizing Framework
detail.abstract:
For three decades, the conventional guidance on gold in an investment portfolio has converged on a narrow range: five to fifteen percent, held primarily as a tail-risk hedge or inflation buffer. That guidance rested on a coherent analytical framework. This paper examines four developments — each documented, each dated — that have materially altered the premises underlying that framework.

First, the gold-TIPS valuation model that anchored conventional sizing experienced a significant structural break on February 24, 2022, when the freezing of Russian central bank assets disrupted the relationship between gold and real interest rates. Second, central banks have migrated from hedging with gold to holding it as a co-equal monetary reserve asset; gold reached 27 percent of global official reserves at end-2025 — partly reflecting price appreciation — surpassing US Treasury holdings at 22 percent for the first time. Third, Basel III’s Net Stable Funding Ratio introduced an 85 percent funding penalty on unallocated and synthetic gold positions while leaving physical gold facing no equivalent treatment, creating a durable structural incentive toward physical accumulation. Fourth, leading institutional research has explicitly retired the commodity taxonomy for gold, characterizing it instead as a monetary asset in the current geopolitical and fiscal environment.

Taken together, these developments do not merely revise the case for gold — they collectively supersede the analytical framework on which conventional sizing rested. This paper does not conclude that outcomes are certain or that the conventional framework produced wrong answers; it concludes that the framework was solving a correctly-specified problem whose premises no longer apply. The question of how much gold belongs portfolio, under a different objective function, is the subject of a companion paper.

title: The Two Sides of a Coin: Perceived and Objective Energy Literacy for Technology Adoption
affiliations: University of Luxembourg - Interdisciplinary Centre for Security, Reliability and Trust (SnT), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Two Sides of a Coin: Perceived and Objective Energy Literacy for Technology Adoption
detail.abstract: Residential electrification through energy technologies such as electric vehicles, photovoltaic systems, and energy storage and smart charging solutions is a key element of the energy transition. While prior research has analyzed the role of objective energy literacy and perceived knowledge in shaping individual’s decisions in other contexts, little is known about their effects on household energy technology uptake. Using a representative household survey of 1,011 respondents in Luxembourg, this paper examines how objective and perceived energy literacy jointly influence the adoption of residential energy technologies. We first show that both objective and perceived energy literacy are positively associated with the probability of adopting at least one energy technology. However, the two dimensions are substantially misaligned: nearly 70% of respondents overestimate their objective energy knowledge. Exploiting this miscalibration, we distinguish between over-estimators, under-estimators, and well-calibrated individuals. We find that adoption behavior among mis-calibrated individuals is less systematic, whereas calibrated energy literacy exhibits a clear and robust positive relationship with technology uptake. Our findings show that energy literacy is not a unidimensional construct and that confidence in one’s knowledge is as important as knowledge itself. From a policy perspective, the results suggest that interventions aimed solely at increasing factual knowledge may be insufficient. Effective policy design should also target the calibration of beliefs, for instance through feedback mechanisms, self-assessment tools, and decision-support instruments that help households better align perceived and actual energy knowledge.

detail.abstract:
This study analyzes 97,028 consumer complaints filed with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) between January 2021 and December 2025 against eleven major US consumer fintechs, classifying each complaint by whether it describes a pattern consistent with a reconciliation failure. Reconciliation is defined as the process of confirming that two or more records of the same money movement agree; a reconciliation failure occurs when those records diverge and the discrepancy produces a consumer-visible outcome such as a transfer that never arrives, a duplicate charge that is not reversed, or a refund that does not post.

The central finding is that reconciliation-related complaints close with CFPB-recorded monetary relief at 9.96%, compared to 3.51% for all other fintech payment complaints in the dataset, a gap of nearly three times. Monetary relief in CFPB terminology means the company paid the consumer to resolve the dispute: a refund, restitution payment, or fee reversal. It is the strongest resolution outcome recorded by the CFPB and reflects a company determination, made under regulatory review, that the consumer was owed money. The near-3x gap holds in direction across all four product categories in the dataset, with reconciliation-related complaints receiving monetary relief at higher rates than non-reconciliation complaints in every category, and relief ratios ranging from 1.4x to 4.0x depending on product type.

In 2021 through 2024, prior to a regulatory event that inflated 2025 complaint volume approximately sevenfold, reconciliation-related complaints represented between 12.95% and 15.64% of all fintech payment complaints annually, with a pooled four-year share of 14.39%, or roughly one in seven. The 2025 data are included in full for transparency and excluded from prevalence estimates; the rationale is detailed in Section 5.

Classification was performed by a reasoning-capable large language model using chain-ofthought prompting. Validation against 80 hand-labeled complaints produced accuracy of 88.75% (95% CI: 80.0%-94.0%), precision of 89.19% (95% CI: 75.3%-95.7%), recall of 86.84% (95% CI: 72.7%-94.2%), specificity of 90.48% (95% CI: 77.9%-96.2%), and F1 of 88.00%. All confidence intervals use the Wilson method (Wilson, 1927). Precision and recall are balanced, indicating the classifier neither systematically over-flags nor under-flags. The full classified dataset, validation set, and CFPB source query are published for independent audit.

The proliferation of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains has driven the development of a sophisticated computational trust ecosystem, encompassing cybersecurity, observability, explainability, provenance, governance, auditability, and compliance systems. Yet these established categories, while indispensable, were designed to address fundamentally different questions than the one increasingly demanded by regulators, courts, auditors, and the public: Can a computational decision be authoritatively verified under the precise conditions (information, policies, model state, and system environment) that existed at the moment it was made? 
This paper builds directly on Constitutional Replay-Authority (Otto, 2026), which defined the proposed infrastructure category dedicated to computational legitimacy and replay verification. The present paper identifies and analyzes the specific infrastructure deficiency-the Computational Legitimacy Gap-that necessitates that category. Drawing on a categorytheoretic analysis and recent developments in AI regulation and verifiable systems (2025-2026), the paper demonstrates that existing categories are categorically misaligned with long-term legitimacy requirements. As model evolution, policy drift, and extended accountability horizons intensify, Constitutional Replay-Authority is positioned as the dedicated categorical response to this previously under-recognized structural challenge.

title: InvEvolve: Evolving White-box Inventory Policies via Large Language Models with Performance Guarantees

detail.title: InvEvolve: Evolving White-box Inventory Policies via Large Language Models with Performance Guarantees
detail.abstract: We study how large language models can be used to generate inventory policies in online settings with non-stationary demand. Our work is motivated by recent advances in LLM-based evolutionary search, such as AlphaEvolve, which demonstrates strong performance on static and highly structured problems such as mathematical discovery, but is not directly suited to dynamic inventory settings with online updates. We propose InvEvolve, an end-to-end inventory policy evolution and inference framework grounded in confidenceinterval-based certification. Built on a large language model trained via reinforcement learning, InvEvolve can process demand data together with additional numerical and textual features, and generates white-box inventory policies with statistical safety guarantees for future deployment. We further introduce a unified framework with theoretical guarantees that connects training, inference, and deployment. This allows us to derive a lower bound on the probability that InvEvolve evolves a statistically safe and improved policy, and to characterize the multi-period performance gap relative to the oracle-safe benchmark. Tested on both synthetic data and real-world retail data, InvEvolve outperforms classical inventory policies and deep-learning-based methods. In canonical inventory settings, it generates new policies that outperform existing benchmarks.

detail.abstract: Organizational culture is the invisible infrastructure of any institution. It includes the shared values, assumptions, norms, and behaviors that shape how people interact, make decisions, and get work done. A central design challenge for an organization pursuing enduring impact is how to build and maintain an organizational culture that is not only mission-aligned but also sufficiently durable and adaptive to sustain meaningful impact over extended periods of time across shifting markets, evolving stakeholder expectations, and changing leadership. This article argues that the most effective culture for an enduring impact organization is an integrated and interdependent system of cultural elements including purpose, stakeholder orientation, learning, integrity, collaboration, inclusion, accountability, and resilience. It further suggests that an enduring impact organization does not conform neatly to any single traditional culture type; rather, it reflects a deliberately constructed hybrid that integrates complementary attributes from multiple cultural paradigms including purpose culture, the adaptive capacity of learning culture, the people-first emphasis of clan culture, and selective aspects of adhocracy culture related to innovation, flexibility, and responsiveness.

title: From Square Law to Swarm Law: A Drone-extended Lanchester Model and the New Mathematics of Attrition across Eight Conflicts

detail.title: From Square Law to Swarm Law: A Drone-extended Lanchester Model and the New Mathematics of Attrition across Eight Conflicts

detail.abstract:
Classical attrition theory treats war as a contest of aggregated firepower: Lanchester's square law rewards concentration, and the side that can mass the most lethal units fastest prevails (Lanchester, 1916; Osipov, 1915). The cheap drone unsettles that arithmetic. 

A first-person-view quadcopter costing a few hundred dollars now destroys armour priced in the millions, while interceptor missiles costing more than the threats they defeat exhaust magazines that cannot be reloaded under fire. This paper argues that drones do not overturn Lanchester's laws; they re-parameterise them. 

It sets out a Drone-Extended Lanchester Model (DELM) that adds a third force vector-mass-produced uncrewed systems-to the classical dyad, drawing on the three-sided combat formalism of Kress, Caulkins, Feichtinger, Grass and Seidl (2018), and makes the effectiveness coefficients endogenous to costexchange ratios and electronic-warfare attrition. 

The framework is applied, in a mutually-exclusive and collectively-exhaustive fashion, to eight contemporary theatres. The central finding is that the outcome of a drone-saturated war is governed less by tactical skill, or even by the cost-exchange revolution itself, than by production depth-the rate at which each side can manufacture and field expendable systems. 

Where defenders trade expensive interceptors against cheap mass, they win engagements while losing the exchange. Tipping-point dynamics are presented as explicitly analytical outputs under structured uncertainty, not forecasts. The policy implication follows directly from the mathematics: in the age of the swarm, the decisive strategic reserve is a factory, not a stockpile.

title: Green Industrialization and Development in Africa: A Conceptual Framework
affiliations: Georgetown University

detail.title: Green Industrialization and Development in Africa: A Conceptual Framework
detail.abstract: The global salience of climate change as a policy concern means that low-income countries are likely to be pressured to adopt development strategies that, where possible, conserve natural resources and minimize greenhouse gas emissions. The African Green Industrialization Initiative (AGII) is an effort to this end. This paper articulates a conceptual framework to guide the implementation of green industrialization strategies in Africa. The main argument is that green industrialization should not be viewed as "greening business-as-usual" but as a techno-industrial step change that enables African countries to exploit energy technologies of the future in pursuit of structural transformation of their economies (i.e., developmentalist green industrialization). The paper then discusses specific policy approaches that African countries can adopt at the sectoral, national, regional, and global levels to advance a developmentalist green industrialization agenda.

title: Banking Adoption in Andhra Pradesh: A Sub-District Level Analysis Using 2011 Census Data

detail.title: Banking Adoption in Andhra Pradesh: A Sub-District Level Analysis Using 2011 Census Data
detail.abstract: In 2011, millions of households in Andhra Pradesh lacked access to the formal banking system. This paper examines what predicted banking adoption at the household level, using OLS regression on 2011 Census data across 1,128 sub-districts. Two explanatory variables, Mobile phone penetration (β = 0.346) and computer and internet access (β = 0.607), were found to be strongly associated with higher banking rates, even after controlling for literacy, urban ratio, and sex ratio. The internet effect, however, was mainly observed among mandals who had better digital access. The findings suggest that digital infrastructure, especially mobile ownership, drove banking adoption in Andhra Pradesh. A possible future extension is to use 2027 census data (as and when it becomes available) to study policy impacts and gender gaps.

title: Pollution Control Under Uncertainty: Integrating Optimal Control Theory and Value of Information
affiliations: , , Bielefeld University - Department of Business Administration and Economics and

detail.title: Pollution Control Under Uncertainty: Integrating Optimal Control Theory and Value of Information
detail.abstract: This study analyses the economic value of information in dynamic environmental decision-making, focusing on how pre-decision resolution of parameter risk affects optimal policy paths. We develop a framework that integrates optimal control (OC) theory with the Value of Information (VoI) concept. Using a continuous-time pollution control model, we analytically derive VoI for different types of uncertainty - initial conditions and model parameters - highlighting how the structure of uncertainty affects its value. We introduce a benchmark "naive certainty-equivalent" policy that ignores uncertainty and quantify the resulting excess in the expected value of perfect information. Our results show that VoI depends on whether uncertainty changes the marginal intertemporal trade-off faced by the decision maker. Information about the initial pollution stock has no value in the present linear-quadratic setting, because it affects welfare levels but not the optimal policy path. By contrast, information about the environmental absorption rate has strictly positive value for any non-degenerate distribution, because it changes the effective persistence of pollution and therefore the optimal balance between current production and future environmental damages. The proposed approach provides a tractable and extensible method for quantifying VoI in intertemporal environmental management problems under parametric risk.
