title: Nonlinear Pricing and Revealed Salience
affiliations: , Bocconi University and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: Nonlinear Pricing and Revealed Salience
detail.abstract: On a major e-commerce platform, we randomize linear promotions applying a δ% discount and nonlinear ones applying the same discount above a spending threshold of M€. We unveil a striking fact: nonlinear schemes create bunching at M but no global self-selection above M relative to linear schemes with the same discount δ. This pattern rejects optimization frictions and standard biases. We offer a salience account: upon seeing (M, δ) some people overly focus on M and cut spending above M (where the threshold should not matter), others overly focus on δ and seek discounts below M (where they do not qualify). Using browsing data on attempts to redeem promotions below M, we confirm the model's predictions and show its ability to match the spending anomalies.

title:
Generative Humanity:
A Framework for Human Flourishing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title:
Generative Humanity:
A Framework for Human Flourishing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence presents a governance challenge that existing frameworks consistently mischaracterize. Regulatory, ethical, and social frameworks overwhelmingly treat AI as a powerful artifact — a tool whose risks can be assessed at the point of deployment and managed through output-level oversight. This paper argues that AI is better understood as a generative process: a complex adaptive system that participates in reshaping the social, epistemic, and ecological conditions within which it operates, rather than merely responding to pre-existing ones. That distinction is not semantic. It is the difference between governing a hammer and governing a river.

Drawing on three converging bodies of original work — generative dynamics, a theory of how complex adaptive systems produce outcomes through multiplicative rather than additive interaction; the epistemological boundaries of machine knowledge, a rigorous account of the four structural knowledge domains permanently inaccessible to AI systems; and cognitive gain-of-function augmentation, a framework for AI as amplifier rather than substitute for human capacity — this paper develops a comprehensive framework for understanding and governing AI's effects on human flourishing.

The paper introduces and develops several original contributions: the pantheistic fallacy, describing the normalized tendency to defer to AI outputs as oracular without epistemic scrutiny; epistemic atrophy, the gradual diminishment of human cognitive capacity through systematic disuse; the generative commons doctrine, extending the principle of the universal destination of goods from static resources to the feedback loops that determine what AI systems become; and a detailed governance architecture proposal centered on a Generative Commons DAO, designed to address the capture, legitimacy, and coordination failures of existing AI governance institutions.

The framework addresses AI's effects on cognition, work, learning, data governance, ecological stewardship, and democratic culture, and develops actor-specific recommendations for governments, technology developers, educational institutions, civil society, researchers, and individuals. A glossary of 46 key terms supports cross-disciplinary accessibility.

title: Product Design under Consumer Rebellion and Preference Uncertainty
affiliations: South China University of Technology - School of Business Administration (SBA),  and School of Business Administration, South China University of Technology

detail.title: Product Design under Consumer Rebellion and Preference Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Consumers increasingly rebel against preference norms to signal individuality. Yet firms facing such rebellion sometimes differentiate their designs whereas sometimes converge to similar designs. How such rebellion shapes product design and differentiation is not well understood, especially when firms are uncertain about consumer preferences and the resulting norm. We develop a gametheoretic model in which two firms choose horizontal designs before preferences are realized and compete in prices afterward. We demonstrate that rebellion exerts a U-shaped impact on equilibrium differentiation. The pattern reflects two opposing effects. Rebellion directly rewards distinctiveness, encouraging differentiation. At the same time, rebellion erodes the consumer-population heterogeneity created by preference uncertainty. Under uncertainty, each firm serves a partially captive consumer segment, which softens competition. Rebellion undermines this captive demand by intensifying consumer switching and firm poaching, thereby inducing firms to offer less differentiated designs. When rebellion is mild, the heterogeneity-eroding effect dominates; when strong, the distinctivenessrewarding effect dominates. Prices and profits also exhibit U-shaped relationships with consumer rebellion; consumer surplus follows an inverted U-shape. Furthermore, compared with the no-rebellion benchmark, a differentiation trap arises: an intermediate level of rebellion leads to greater product differentiation, but lower firm profits and consumer surplus, in contrast to the classical wisdom that greater differentiation indicates higher profits.

title: Plastic Dumping Grounds: The International Incidence of Environmental Regulation
affiliations: , Univeristy of Oxford and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Plastic Dumping Grounds: The International Incidence of Environmental Regulation
detail.abstract: Environmental regulations often generate environmental improvements at home, yet their consequences may extend far beyond the countries that adopt them. The international incidence of environmental regulation remains poorly understood. We study where the resulting environmental damages emerge and who ultimately bears their costs using China's 2017 ban on waste imports, which triggered a large reallocation of global recycling activity. Combining international trade data, administrative records, direct measures of firms' waste mismanagement, and local pollution data in the main destination for diverted waste, we examine the international incidence of environmental regulation by tracing the rarely observed process linking trade reallocation to firm behavior, pollution exposure, and welfare. The ban increased pollution-intensive plastic waste imports, lowering input costs for downstream firms using recyclable materials. Meanwhile, imported waste displaced domestic recyclables, leading firms to adopt harmful disposal methods. The environmental damages from air pollution exceeded the economic gains from access to lower-cost inputs.

title: Public Expenditure Shocks and Human Capital Development in the Presence of Structural Breaks: Evidence from Nigeria
affiliations: RadarMetrics Research & Advisory, RadarMetrics Research & Advisory Inc and

detail.title: Public Expenditure Shocks and Human Capital Development in the Presence of Structural Breaks: Evidence from Nigeria
detail.abstract: The study examines the impact of public expenditure shocks on human capital development in in the Presence of Structural Breaks: Evidence from Nigeria. The nature of this study necessitates the use of a time-series research design and an extensive reliance on secondary data sourced from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) statistical bulletins, for the period 1981-2018. The method of data analysis utilized a battery of econometric applications often used in most contemporary economic time-series studies. First, the descriptive and correlation analysis is presented. After that the Augmented Dickey Fuller (ADF) unit root test and Zivot and Andrews Unit root for structural breaks is applied and this is followed by the co-integration test both with and without structural breaks. The Wald test for significance of the structural breaks was also employed and then the Variance Autoregressive (VAR) technique is then utilized. Finally, the impulse-response functions is conducted The study findings reveal that response of HCAP to innovations in HEXP is shown to exhibit oscillations over the period horizon with initial declines showing in the 1 st quarter after the shock. An immediate rebound in HCAP response is observed beginning from the 2 nd quarter after the shock and this positive rebound is sustained up to 10 th quarter after the shock. However, one standard deviation shocks to EDEXP is seen to have immediate positive effects on HCAP lasting till 2-3 quarters after the shock and then followed by a decline sustained at a little below the baseline and declining further in the 7 th quarter but again we see a slight rebound which reverts. On the overall, the shocks shows high potentials for asymptotic convergence and stability in HCAP. However, the response of HCAP to investment shocks is the most destabilizing. Furthermore, we observe that the impulse response functions are robust to structural breaks. The evidence of structural breaks reveals few instances of variations with the main analysis without breaks especially in relation the public expenditure. The result shows that, with the inclusion of breaks, the sustained positive effect in HCAP of a one standard deviation shock in HEXP is still observed and also sustained up to 10 th quarter after the shock. Again just like in the case of no structural breaks, we also find that the shocks in EDEXP shows high potentials for asymptotic convergence and stability in the response of HCAP but in the case of investment, we find some differences in the response of HCAP comparing with and without structural breaks. The study recommends that need for government to ensure efficiency in public expenditures.

title: Frictions in News Consumption: Evidence from Social Media
affiliations: Bocconi University, Tel Aviv University and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: Frictions in News Consumption: Evidence from Social Media
detail.abstract: We study the drivers of like-minded and low-reliability news-following on social media, and the effectiveness of interventions targeting them. In a five-week field experiment with more than 3,000 U.S. Facebook users, we document the passive nature of participants' news portfolio formation process and the role of behavioral frictions. The experiment varies whether participants are prompted to re-optimize the portfolio of news pages they follow on Facebook through a user-friendly platform-integrated interface, and whether they receive personalized information about outlet slant and reliability. In contrast to canonical models of news consumption, we find that the re-optimization interface induces large portfolio changes even without new information, while information alone has no effect unless paired with re-optimization. Our interventions produce two main effects: they reduce the slant and increase the reliability of users' portfolios, thus potentially mitigating negative externalities for democracy, and they move users' portfolios closer to their stated preferences, mitigating internalities.

title: AI Impact on Executive-level Jobs Performance: A Literature Review

detail.title: AI Impact on Executive-level Jobs Performance: A Literature Review
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has changed from being a nice to have to be a fundamental capability that changed how executives conduct work across all industries. This paper reviews the growing empirical evidence on how AI is changing executive-level job performance, with particular attention to decision-making, leadership, strategic management, and the reshaping of managerial skills. Inspecting studies in upper echelons theory, the resourcebased view, and the dynamic managerial capability perspective, the paper reviews thirty studies published between 2019 and 2026 in leading management, economics, and information systems journals. The review reaches a conclusion that AI, especially generative AI, leads to substantial productivity gains at the task level, shrinks the productivity gap between newer and more experienced knowledge workers, and accelerates strategic decision-making. Executive work is not simply being augmented, it is being reformed. Top management teams now face new demands for AI literacy, ethical stewardship, cross-functional orchestration, and the design of hybrid human-AI decision-making processes. The reviewed studies demonstrate that executives tend to rely on AI advice in strategic contexts, that algorithm aversion persists in high-stakes settings, and that human-AI collaboration produces superior outcomes only under specific task and delegation conditions. The literature also documents how executive AI adoption is significantly associated with firm-level performance outcomes such as innovation, sales growth, and operating efficiency. The review identifies four recurring themes across the literature which are AI's effect on executive decision-making, the redefinition of executive skills and capabilities, the mediating role of AI in leader-employee relationships, and AI's impact on firm-level outcomes. The paper closes with implications drawn from the reviewed evidence and an agenda for future research, suggesting that executives in the AI era are being asked to lead in substantively new ways rather than being displaced by intelligent systems.

title: Relational Dignity Infrastructure - The Human Layer Required to Make Material Housing Inhabitable
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Relational Dignity Infrastructure - The Human Layer Required to Make Material Housing Inhabitable
detail.abstract: Material housing provision does not produce human recovery. Finland's Housing First infrastructure achieves eighty to ninety percent two-year retention; the United States achieves below forty percent. The difference is not the housing unit. It is the ambient relational environment within and surrounding that unit at the moment of occupancy. This paper defines Relational Dignity Infrastructure (RDI) as the systematically designed, continuously operating social environment that produces ontological security, identity capital accumulation, and the functional capacity for reintegration that material shelter alone cannot generate. RDI is positioned as the third operational layer of a three-part dignity stack: Material Dignity Infrastructure (MDI) delivers biological survival conditions; RDI delivers the relational recognition and social continuity required for selfhood persistence; identity capital accumulation delivers the agentive selfhood required for reintegration into civic life. Drawing on Giddens's ontological security framework, Porges's polyvagal theory, Padgett's social-material conjunction findings, Cote and Levine's identity capital theory, Tsai and colleagues' social integration evidence, and the Y-Foundation's operational documentation of the Finnish national Housing First system, the paper establishes RDI as a formal theoretical construct and maps its five production conditions onto the existing MDI tower architecture: Dunbar-scale pod environments, the live-in Pod Steward role, peer support workforce deployment, the unconditional Ground Floor Commons, and recurring community practice mechanisms including the Pod Council and common kitchen. Two integration gaps requiring specification are identified: the relational intake protocol, grounded in polyvagal neuroception architecture, and the social network transition protocol, specified through Social Network Analysis methodology. Five RDI verification metrics are proposed as leading indicators of the eight binary material metrics that constitute the MDI Singular Prototype Threshold. The RDI workforce layer is positioned as a revenue-generating clinical infrastructure component billable under California's CalAIM Enhanced Care Management and In Lieu of Services frameworks, converting the relational layer from a cost center into a MediCal revenue stream under existing state law.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Audit Quality on Accounting Anomalies: Evidence from Stock Exchange
affiliations: Islamic Azad University

detail.title: Analyzing the Impact of Audit Quality on Accounting Anomalies: Evidence from Stock Exchange
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of audit quality components on accounting anomalies within the context of predicting business failure. Drawing from a mixed-method empirical study on companies listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange, this article analyzes data from 164 managers and accountants. Grounded in a research model that identified 17 key components of accounting anomalies and corporate governance, the study specifically tests the influence of three core audit quality indicators-auditor-specific characteristics, the audit process, and audit outcomes-on accounting anomalies. The findings reveal that auditor-specific characteristics and audit results have a significant and negative effect on reducing accounting anomalies, thereby enhancing the accuracy of business failure prediction. However, the audit process, as defined in this study, did not show a statistically significant impact. The results underscore the crucial role of high-quality auditing, particularly auditor expertise and the informational value of audit reports, in mitigating earnings management, reducing discretionary accruals, and promoting overall financial reporting quality.

Although originally well-intended, these practices spark controversy over privacy, human rights and fairness and raise questions regarding the lack of accountability for their potential negative impacts. As these challenges are caused by a “web” of interrelated decisions taken by organisations, individuals, regulators and academics, a comprehensive understanding of accountability is a digital era requires integration of knowledge and insight from multiple disciplines. We rely on a basic model for accountability which is conceptually rooted in the principal-agent model and analyse the implications of big data and AI for accountability for different stakeholder groups.

title: Retained Complexity at Its Limits: Carrying Capacity, Internal Coordination Exploitation, and System Stability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Retained Complexity at Its Limits: Carrying Capacity, Internal Coordination Exploitation, and System Stability
detail.abstract: This paper develops a formal framework for retained complexity: the stock of usable knowledge, procedures, records, standards, and specialist repertoires that a complex coordination system can preserve and reproduce over time. Retained complexity is modeled as an accumulation-loss balance in which productive novelty, effective cultural population, retention fidelity, and integration payoff compete against local attrition, structural discontinuity, external exploitation, and internal coordination exploitation. The framework's central claim is that mature coordination systems generate exploitable internal disturbance variety through their own rules, records, interfaces, permissions, classifications, and validation procedures. As coordination-surface burden rises, generative search capacity can increasingly be redirected toward exploiting the system's own coordination architecture rather than extending productive complexity. The paper derives retained-complexity carrying-capacity, specialization, viability, and internal-stability conditions; develops a formal coordination-exploitation mechanism; and analyzes how support-throughput and knowledge-carrying thresholds alter the sustainable complexity of systems that depend on retained information. Simulations compare the mechanism against alternative null models, and a worked empirical operationalization uses corporate tax-complexity data to illustrate architecture-dependent internal exploitation and model-completeness constraints. The framework generates falsifiable predictions concerning institutional fragility, coordination burden, endogenous exploitation, and the scaling limits of complex systems.

title: Reporting Effectiveness Results in Meta-Analyses
affiliations: Kühne Logistics University

detail.title: Reporting Effectiveness Results in Meta-Analyses
detail.abstract: Due to its comparability across studies, the most often applied effect-size measure in meta-analyses is the correlation coefficient. While in psychology researchers want to know whether a relationship between variables exists, the majority of researchers in marketing (except for consumer research) want to report on the overall effectiveness or impact of one variable on another across published studies. Effectiveness is measured by the regression coefficient, which can be made comparable across studies by calculating corresponding elasticities that can be directly applied to optimization approaches. Nevertheless, many effectiveness-oriented meta-analyses use correlation coefficients as an effectiveness measure, although correlations provide only information about the strength of the statistical association between two variables and the degree of confidence in it. This is due to the high availability of correlations in studies and the situation that elasticities can only be calculated for ratio-scaled variables such as money and effort. Many marketing effectiveness studies, however, use interval scales for constructs such as selling orientation, customer satisfaction, or agility. As relative changes are arbitrary there, I suggest pseudo-elasticities as effect-size measures where the regression coefficients are first transformed as if they were coming from the normalized data range of 0-1, which can be achieved via the scale length. Second, these normalized regression coefficients are then relativized by the means of the dependent and independent variables, as is done for elasticities. The proposal distinguishes among three cases: first, where both the dependent and independent variables are interval-scaled; second, where the dependent variable, such as sales performance, is ratio-scaled but the independent variable is interval-scaled; and third, where the independent variable is binary, as in experiments. This will allow meta-analysts to report effectiveness information rather than only correlations.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is transforming work not only by automating tasks, but by redistributing judgment, discretion, learning opportunities, accountability, and visibility. Existing theories of psychological safety, technology acceptance, trust in AI, job design, and algorithmic management explain important parts of this transformation, but they do not fully explain whether employees feel safe to challenge AI outputs, disclose AI use, report AI errors, contest inappropriate automated decisions, or preserve human agency under large-scale AI adoption. This paper develops Algorithmic Psychological Safety Climate (APSC) as a domain-specific extension of Edmondson’s psychological safety theory for AI-enabled organizations. 

Drawing on a scoping review and integrative theory development, the paper positions APSC within a broader Human Capital Governance Framework. The theory argues that AI creates value or harm through human capital allocation: the redistribution of tasks, decision rights, developmental work, and accountability between humans and machines. Poorly governed allocation produces Human Hollowing: erosion of human judgment, skill, agency, dignity, meaning, and employability. Human Capital Governance is introduced as the missing organizational mechanism that protects and renews human capability through capability audits, reskilling, appeal rights, human fallback, participatory design, and non-punitive AI voice systems. The paper offers definitions, propositions, discriminant-validity arguments, and a future research agenda. It contributes a mid-range theory explaining how organizations can adopt AI while preserving psychological safety, human capability, and responsible employee voice.

detail.abstract: This study examines the theoretical implications of AI-driven predictive analytics adoption among small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the United Kingdom. The research employs an interpretivist philosophy, inductive approach, and secondary qualitative research design to explore factors influencing adoption and organisational outcomes. The study analyses existing literature using thematic analysis and evaluates adoption through the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) Framework, Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) Theory, and Resource-Based View (RBV). Findings indicate that perceived usefulness, organisational readiness, environmental pressures, innovation characteristics, and strategic capabilities significantly influence adoption. The study contributes to understanding how predictive analytics supports competitiveness, decision-making, and business growth among SMEs.

title: Tokens, Watts, and Geography - AI infrastructure
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Tokens, Watts, and Geography - AI infrastructure
detail.abstract: The sell-side consensus on AI infrastructure prices capex in absolute terms — six hundred billion here, seven hundred billion there — and prices inference output in narrative terms — “the price of intelligence is collapsing.” Both framings miss the same thing. Inference output is a manufactured good. Its marginal cost is dominated by electricity. And electricity is not priced globally, it is priced by interconnect. This paper develops a four-tier framework for the geographic pricing of AI inference between 2026 and 2030. Tier 1 (Sovereign Capable) — China, the Gulf, the Nordic countries, France — combines low marginal electricity cost with state-backed capacity expansion. Tier 2 (Emerging Stretched) — India, South Korea, Japan — has committed hundreds of billions to sovereign compute on grids that are not yet stable enough to clear it. Tier 3 (Power Constrained Wealthy) — the United States in the PJM interconnect, Germany, the United Kingdom — concentrates capex without the physical electricity to dispatch it; PJM has now cleared its annual capacity auction at or near the regulatory cap three years in a row, and the 2027/2028 auction came in short of its reliability target for the first time in the RTO’s history. Tier 4 (Arbitrage Suppliers) — Russian Siberia, Canadian hydro, the Brazilian Norte/Nordeste, Australian Pilbara — owns the cheapest electrons on earth and is now exporting them, increasingly, to Tier 1 workloads via cross-border power agreements and dual-resident cloud structures. We derive a simple unit-economics identity for token output — marginal cost equals energy per token times utilization-adjusted delivered electricity price, plus capex amortization — and quantify the spread across tiers using 2024–2026 data. We then show that Shanghai Futures Exchange’s preliminary AI-token futures, which most coverage treats as a domestic Chinese compute-hedging tool, will function instead as the world’s first tradable instrument on the cross-tier electricity risk premium of AI inference. We close with five testable predictions for Q3 2026 to Q4 2027. We are not arguing that one tier wins. We are arguing that pricing models which ignore the floor are mispriced by an order of magnitude that the market has not yet been forced to confront.

detail.abstract: Human labor is priced by the hour and a language model's output by the token, and firms weigh the two when deciding what to automate. The two carry no fixed exchange rate, since a token is not a fixed quantity of work and a more capable model does more per token, so the threshold at which a unit of work costs less in tokens than in human time must be located rather than assumed. That threshold is the time-token breakeven point, asserted for regulated professional work but not defined. This paper defines it and shows that it is a conditional surface rather than a single number, because the token-side cost turns on the model generation, the token price, and the degree of cost capitalization. The breakeven point moves toward tokens as capital expenditure converts standard-bound judgment into reusable assets at near-zero marginal cost, so the judgment that appears to keep work in human hands is a capitalization lag rather than a floor, giving way faster where the governing standard is more explicit. It is bounded, sitting on the judgment residual alone and unable to cross the relational residual, where the human contribution is itself what the client buys, or the regulatory residual, which the law places on a licensed person and is indifferent to cost. In regulated accounting, where judgment is heavily standard-bound and the relational element is small, the two bounds reduce to one, the signature the law reserves for a licensed person, which holds whatever the token price does and whatever the model can do. The analysis is cost-side, and the paper illustrates the breakeven on three accounting judgments and sets out a design for estimating it from production data, where a verifiable quality bar makes the cost comparison identifiable.

title: Dayenu: The Ancient Jewish Case for Thankfulness and Its Modern Psychological Parallels
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: Dayenu: The Ancient Jewish Case for Thankfulness and Its Modern Psychological Parallels
detail.abstract: Long before positive psychology identified gratitude as a cornerstone of human flourishing, Jewish tradition had already systematized it, embedding thankfulness into daily prayer, religious law, biblical narrative, and Talmudic teaching as a moral and spiritual obligation rather than a polite virtue. This paper traces the evolution of thankfulness across major bodies of Jewish literature, from the Torah and Prophets to the Writings and the Talmud. By examining key case studies such as Leah's naming of Judah, the Todah (thanksgiving) offering, the story of King Hezekiah, and liturgical cornerstones such as Modeh Ani, Nishmat, and the Dayenu prayer, we analyze how ancient texts define and institutionalize appreciation. We pair these traditional sources with contemporary empirical research demonstrating that gratitude enhances life satisfaction and prosocial behavior while actively mitigating depression and materialism. What emerges is not merely a historical parallel but a convergence: both traditions arrived independently at the same conclusion, that gratitude must be practiced deliberately and repeatedly before it becomes a stable disposition, and both devised systematic methods to achieve exactly that. The paper argues that this convergence carries practical consequences for individuals, organizational leaders, and society as a whole.

title: The Mechanics of Failure – An Integrated Analysis of Governance Drift to Systemic Breakdown

detail.title: The Mechanics of Failure – An Integrated Analysis of Governance Drift to Systemic Breakdown
detail.abstract:
This paper presents an integrated analysis of governance drift to systemic breakdown, drawing together six independent papers published between 2022 and 2025. 

It positions governance failure not as an event but a trajectory.  One that organisations traverse incrementally through tolerated ambiguity, narrative substitution, diffused accountability and the normalisation of deviation until departure from standards becomes the standard itself.

The analysis is grounded in direct operational experience of a major corporate governance failure and sustained examination of public post-failure proceedings. Its focus throughout is structural rather than individual: these are not accounts of villains, but examinations of conditions.

The conceptual foundation is a three-conditions  'Pressure, Permission, and Plausibility' developed as an operational reinterpretation of Cressey's fraud triangle, reframed for an organisational and governance focus. 

The six papers examine distinct mechanisms: incentivised ambiguity; structural blind spots in externalised models; the stress-testing of governance narratives under adversarial legal scrutiny; the formalisation of organisational blind spots through AI deployment; the progression from acceptance through normalisation to boundary collapse; and a counterpoint on the governance risks produced by excessive conformance.

A concluding appendix aligns the analysis with established academic theory. Vaughan's normalisation of deviance and structural secrecy, Bandura's moral disengagement, Reason's Swiss Cheese model, Perrow's Normal Accident Theory, and Simon's bounded rationality. Demonstrating that the mechanisms identified through operational experience converge independently with structural explanations developed across organisational theory and systems analysis.

title: Min-Cut Certificates for Process Flexibility: k-Chains and Beyond
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Min-Cut Certificates for Process Flexibility: k-Chains and Beyond
detail.abstract: We develop a min-cut certificate approach to sparse process-flexibility design. The classical long-chain theory relies on complementarity among flexible arcs, but that mechanism breaks down once each plant can serve three or more products. The replacement is a product-set certificate: a low-demand set is costly exactly when it traps too many complete plant neighborhoods. This certificate separates demand risk from topology. Ancillary fixed-design diagnostics relate the same certificate to generalized chaining gaps and marginal-sales certificates. For chain designs with a fixed neighborhood degree, the certificate becomes an interval problem, which gives finite-size monotonicity, normalized risk-pooling monotonicity, diminishing returns in the flexibility degree, and efficient finite-system computation. The same certificate also explains when chains are the wrong topology. Exact pair-spread designs are certificate-profile optimal for all small bottleneck sets q<2k-1. For projective-plane designs with n=k^2-k+1, this distribution-free profile result yields a coefficient separation under binary 0/2 demand: the design improves on the k-chain by n(k-2)p^{k+1}(1-p)^{n-k-1}+O(p^{k+2}), with the Fano-plane theorem as the k = 3 instance. Numerical experiments show that low-codegree balanced topologies improve on chain designs in general.

title: Reconnecting Federal Law and the Common Law
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: Reconnecting Federal Law and the Common Law
detail.abstract:
This Article provides the first detailed account of a crucial phenomenon in American law: the federal law–common law disconnect. Throughout history, the Constitution and other federal texts have relied on common law concepts; the federal courts routinely adjudicate common law questions, no less than constitutional or statutory ones; and practically and culturally, the United States is a common law country, just like the rest of its Anglo-American peers. Today, motivated by an array of factors ranging from legal realism to originalism, many federal judges and practitioners exhibit a deep aversion toward the common law, perceiving it at best as a matter that should be left to state courts. When faced with common law cases (as they constantly are), these members of the federal legal community often turn to free-floating methods of reasoning, which misconstrue core principles of multiple areas of law, generate plainly unjust and inefficient outcomes, and subvert, rather than promote, both realist and originalist commitments.

In the process of uncovering the federal law–common law disconnect, this Article makes four main contributions to the literature, which innovatively bring together multiple spaces of recent scholarship, from constitutional law and the new originalism, through law and economics, to private law theory. First, the Article explores the common law origins of the American legal system, at both the state and federal level. Second, it identifies the primary drivers of the rift that has, nonetheless, developed between the federal legal system and the common law. Third, it ties together a broad, trans-substantive group of recent cases—from the Purdue bankruptcy litigation to the Supreme Court’s decisions on corporate personhood—where this disconnect has led to both injustice, inefficiency, and divergence from the historical meaning of legal norms. Fourth, it proposes in detail how federal law and the common law can and must reconnect, thus setting a crucial segment of our legal system on a more historically, textually, economically, and morally tenable path forward.

detail.abstract:
Background: Nursing research is expanding rapidly in Morocco, yet evidence on how ethical standards are understood, applied, and reported remains scarce. We aimed to assess research ethics knowledge among nurses and evaluate the quality of ethics reporting in nursing studies involving human participants.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey among Moroccan nurses and trainees (n=290) to examine ethics training, knowledge, and research practices. In parallel, we performed a meta-research analysis of nursing publications with human data (n=105; 2022-2025), assessing reporting of ethics approval, informed consent, data protection, and overall ethics reporting quality. A multivariable logistic regression model was used to identify factors associated with optimal ethics knowledge.

Findings: Although most participants recognized key ethical requirements, half reported conducting research without ethics committee approval, and only 19% demonstrated adequate overall knowledge. Among published studies, most reported informed consent and ethics approval; however, reporting was often incomplete, and only 38% met criteria for optimal ethics. In multivariable analyses, research ethics education during advanced training (adjusted OR=2.72) and awareness of article retraction risk (adjusted OR=2.14) were associated with optimal ethics knowledge. Open peer-review was associated with optimal ethics reporting (OR=3.71).

Interpretation: Gaps persist between awareness, practice, and reporting of research ethics in Moroccan nursing research. These findings highlight the need for strengthened ethics training and better institutional oversight to improve both research practice and reporting. Similar challenges are likely to affect other low- and middle-income settings undergoing rapid research expansion.

detail.title: Fight Fire With Fire: How Does AI-Powered Technology Empower the Elderly Anti-AI Fraud Through a Socio-Technical Systems Theory Lens?

detail.abstract: As digital fraud increasingly exploits artificial intelligence (AI), the elderly, due to their limited digital literacy and declining cognitive abilities, have become vulnerable targets. This paper examines how AI technology enables the elderly to protect themselves from online fraud stemming from complex technologies through the lens of socio-technical system (STS) theory. Using the “Silver Guardian” project, developed under the Cyber-Shield Security Ecosystem of a Chinese company, as an example, this study explores the effectiveness of jointly optimizing the technical and social subsystems within the STS to tailor anti-fraud products for elderly consumers. Throughout the stages of product formation, iteration, and upgrading to cloud-based prevention, the AI-based anti-fraud technology subsystem is aligned with the social subsystem of the elderly, characterized by low digital literacy, high emotional vulnerability, and specific cognitive limitations, achieving a progressive development of the consumer-brand relationship from ability and benevolence to integrity trust, via a “controlled, cooperative, and evaluative” iterative algorithm governance model. This significantly enhances the product's technical performance and reduces the AI fraud risk for the elderly at each stage. Theoretically, this study synthesizes prior work on consumer fraud, elderly vulnerability, AI as a double-edged sword, and STST, advancing understanding of consumer well-being and theoretical disclosures on vulnerable consumers, proposes an integrative socio-technical framework that moves beyond fragmented perspectives to optimize technical and social subsystems, and forms a novel theoretical lens extending in consumer behavior, algorithmic governance, and brand trust, offering a holistic explanation of AI's dual role in exploiting and protecting vulnerable populations. Practically, by understanding the dual role of AI in both promoting and combating fraud, this study develops a generalized roadmap, and suggests technical and policy intervention directions to protect vulnerable groups from AI fraud.

title: Revisiting Consumer Ethnocentric Tendency amid Deglobalization: A Political Narrative Perspective

detail.title: Revisiting Consumer Ethnocentric Tendency amid Deglobalization: A Political Narrative Perspective
detail.abstract:
Purpose
This research aims to develop and test a new theoretical framework for ethnocentric consumption, highlighting the influence of political narratives in the age of deglobalization.

Design/methodology/approach
Building on narrative transportation theory and master narrative engagement research, this research advances an integrated framework to delineate the distinct pathways through which two pervasive political narratives—patriotic and nationalistic—influence ethnocentric consumption. Covariance-based structural equation modelling was employed to analyze online survey data from a diverse sample of Chinese consumers (n = 800) representing 24 provinces and autonomous regions and capturing different demographic characteristics (in terms of gender, age, income, and education).

Findings
The findings reveal that Chinese consumers’ transportation into political narratives strengthens belief in patriotic (nationalistic) narratives, which in turn fosters adoption of supportive (competitive) ideology. Adoption of supportive (competitive) ideology subsequently leads to secure (defensive) national identity, which promotes ethnocentric evaluation (protection) tendency, resulting in ethnocentric consumption characterized by an increased preference and willingness to pay a price premium for domestic (over foreign) brands.

Originality/value
By conceptualizing political narratives as a driver of consumer ethnocentric tendency, this research introduces a novel perspective for understanding how geopolitics impacts consumer behavior. It enriches consumer ethnocentrism and global branding literature, and offers actionable insights for global marketers to design proper branding and advertising strategies amid rising geopolitical risks in the age of deglobalization.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how dividend policy affects shareholder value in leading Indian companies across FMCG, Oil & Gas, IT services, and Banking during 2019-2025. Using secondary data for ITC, Reliance Industries, Infosys, TCS, and HDFC Bank, we analyze trends in Dividend per Share (DPS), Earnings per Share (EPS), and share prices (MPS). Findings support a balanced, stable dividend policy as a meaningful contributor to shareholder value alongside earnings, growth opportunities, liquidity, and market conditions.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a substrate-invariant algebraic framework for modeling the lifecycle of exchange events in open, asynchronous networks. The framework proposes that any atomic exchange event can be characterized by a 6-tuple primitive structure governed by three binary lifecycle dimensions-Recognition, Articulation, and Settlement-producing a closed 16-state combinatoric space. 

Three formal results are established: (1) the strict non-commutativity of lifecycle morphism composition, demonstrating that the ordering of recognition and settlement events determines residual state; (2) the identity preservation and distributivity properties of the covariant projection functor mapping primitive events to macroscopic state; and (3) the emergence of a Persistent Residual Vector whenever lifecycle dimensions are asynchronous, with global conservation following as a structural invariant of the projection. 

The framework is validated in financial systems, where it produces a working accounting state representation demonstrating that standard financial representations emerge from temporal exchange mechanics without domain-specific ontology. A direct engineering application in distributed software systems is developed, where the distributivity property enables consistent global state snapshots without distributed locks. 

The paper closes with a discussion of directions for cross-domain investigation, identifying structural correspondences in quantum information theory, biology, and psychology that warrant future collaborative research but are not developed as formal claims here.

This essay introduces the dominant award procedure in U.S. federal procurement, competitive negotiation under Part 15 of the Federal Acquisition Regulation.  The piece is a primer, descriptive rather than argumentative, and is intended for readers comparing the U.S. system with their own.  After situating competitive negotiation among the other procedures available to federal contracting officers (sealed bidding, simplified acquisition, and sole-source procurement), it walks through the three principal stages of a best-value tradeoff source selection: the preliminary evaluation of proposals against the stated evaluation factors; the decision either to award on initial proposals or to establish a competitive range and conduct negotiations; and the source selection authority's tradeoff decision itself, including the documentation that decision must contain to survive a bid protest.

title: Why Public-private Partnerships Fail: Institutional Constraints and a New Risk-sharing Model

detail.title: Why Public-private Partnerships Fail: Institutional Constraints and a New Risk-sharing Model
detail.abstract: Public-private partnerships have become a central instrument of infrastructure policy across both developed and developing economies, yet their performance record remains contested and their failure rate is high by any reasonable standard. This paper argues that PPP failures stem from two compounding problems that the existing literature tends to treat separately: structural deficiencies in how risks are allocated within PPP contracts, and institutional constraints in the public sector that prevent those contracts from being properly designed, monitored, and enforced. Treating either problem in isolation produces incomplete prescriptions. Evidence from over four decades of PPP experience, including Guasch's (2004) landmark finding that 55 percent of Latin American transport concessions were renegotiated within an average of 2.2 years of award, Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl's (2002) documentation of systematic cost underestimation across transport megaprojects, and the World Bank's Benchmarking Infrastructure Development 2023 assessment of PPP regulatory frameworks across 140 economies, allows for a precise diagnosis of where and why the model breaks down. In response, this paper proposes the Adaptive Risk Allocation Structure (ARAS), a contract design framework that builds pre-specified, automatic risksharing mechanisms into PPP agreements for three primary risk categories: construction cost risk, demand risk, and political risk. ARAS is designed to reduce renegotiation frequency by removing the discretionary gaps that invite opportunistic behavior, while preserving private incentives for efficiency and expanding the range of institutional investors who can participate. A comparative analysis against traditional PPP models and pure availability payment structures shows that ARAS achieves better outcomes across renegotiation resistance, private investor appetite, and fiscal transparency. The paper concludes with implementation guidance and policy recommendations that address the institutional preconditions without which any contract design remains vulnerable.

title: The Computational Minimum Wage: Funding an AI Dividend through Public Ownership of Computational Infrastructure
affiliations: Stanford University

detail.title: The Computational Minimum Wage: Funding an AI Dividend through Public Ownership of Computational Infrastructure
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence advances, computational labor is becoming a close-and at the frontier, near-perfect-substitute for human labor. In a free market, the falling price of computation (Moore's Law) and rising algorithmic capability threaten to erode the demand for human labor and, where substitution is strong, to depress wages sharply. This paper proposes an AI Dividend financed not by taxation but by public ownership of the AI economy's foundational compute layer. Because massscale compute provision is a natural monopoly-vast fixed costs and a marginal cost near the price of electricity, I model it as a public utility run by a Computational Reserve: a monopsony buyer of hardware and the monopoly provider of compute. Pricing above marginal cost recovers the build-out and returns the operating surplus to citizens as a universal dividend. Because compute demand is inelastic through the transition, the dividend-maximizing price sits at or above the human-equivalent wage, so the price that funds the dividend is itself a "Computational Minimum Wage" that slows displacement. I characterize the free-market wage path under finite substitutability, the surplus maximizing price, the dividend's self-sustaining condition, and an import-parity rule for the open economy.

title: Joint Cross-layer Optimisation with Non-convex Stochastic Constraints for Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks under Random Mobility

detail.title: Joint Cross-layer Optimisation with Non-convex Stochastic Constraints for Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks under Random Mobility
detail.abstract: Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks (UWSNs) are a strategic infrastructure for marine surveillance, fisheries monitoring, and early-warning systems along African coastlines. Yet, all existing cross-layer protocols assume that node mobility is deterministic or follows simple memoryless random-walk models, an assumption that breaks down under real oceanic currents. In this paper, we (i) model node mobility as a three-dimensional Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process whose drift and diffusion coefficients are calibrated from HYCOM and Argo oceanographic data, (ii) formulate the joint power-allocation, clustering and TDMA-scheduling problem as a multi-objective Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty (DPP) program with probabilistic chance-constraints over PDR, latency, energy and Age of Information (AoI), (iii) solve it through a distributed primal–dual algorithm coupled with a Dueling Double Deep-Q-Network (D3QN) operating under partial observability (POMDP), and (iv) establish formal convergence and queue-stability guarantees using G/G/1 theory under variable delays. The proposed protocol, SC-LyDQN (Stochastic Cross-layer Lyapunov DQN), is validated through extensive simulation against four baselines (VBF, DBR, EEDBR, DeepAquaNet) on a self-contained underwater testbed reproducing DESERT semantics. Under realistic stochastic mobility (current intensity factor κ up to 2.5), SC-LyDQN raises the average PDR to 0.987 (vs. 0.937 for the strongest deterministic-mobility deep-RL baseline, +5.3%), reduces AoI by over 95%, and shortens end-to-end latency by approximately 25%, while preserving formal queue stability across V parameter sweeps.

delivery, and consumption through chains of mutual obligations rather than relying primarily on
scarce cash liquidity. The paper does not claim that money can be replaced. Instead, it studies a
narrower question: whether economic coordination can continue under liquidity constraints
when obligations are visible, accountable, and linked to expected final demand.
The paper develops a preliminary model of commitment coordination. In this model, participants
record offers, needs, obligations, deadlines, guarantor relationships, fulfillment status, disputes,
and reputation markers in an auditable registry. The proposed SinerGenius pilot is designed as a
small-scale test involving 8-12 entrepreneurs. Its purpose is to examine whether AI-assisted and
auditable infrastructure can reduce the manual coordination bottleneck observed in the
historical case.
The paper also presents preliminary simulation results comparing manual coordination with
auditable commitment coordination. These simulations are not presented as proof of real-world
effectiveness, but as an illustrative model for identifying measurable variables, possible failure
points, and testable hypotheses.
The paper outlines the pilot architecture, commitment accounting logic, anti-favoritism
safeguards, dispute-resolution mechanisms, measurable success and failure criteria, and key
limitations. It argues that the model should be treated as an empirical pilot design rather than a
completed theory or validated economic system.

detail.abstract: The marketing of value-added jackfruit products in Kerala faces persistent challenges despite the crop's immense potential in domestic and international markets (T et al., 2024) 1. Jackfruit chips, flour, halwa, and frozen varieties are in growing demand in markets such as Australia, the USA, and the Middle East. (Corporation, 2026) 2. Previous studies have primarily emphasised issues of limited consumer awareness and inadequate branding; however, a comprehensive analysis of marketing challenges remains limited. The study attempts to fill this gap by dealing with the major constraints like packaging, competition, branding, advertising, pricing and market reach. Data was collected from agro-processing units and analysed using SPSS. Statistical tests like the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test and the Chi-square test were applied to understand the perception and response of processing units towards these constraints. The study finds that branding and advertising are the most important constraints, whereas pricing is a relatively less important constraint. The overall findings suggest that marketing difficulties are moderate across most units. The study contributes to the literature on agro-based product marketing by highlighting priority areas for intervention and providing practical implications for policymakers and entrepreneurs to strengthen the global competitiveness of Kerala's jackfruit industry.

title: When Helpfulness Overrides Causal Caution: Context-Dependent Suppression and Recovery in LLMs

detail.title: When Helpfulness Overrides Causal Caution: Context-Dependent Suppression and Recovery in LLMs
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into decision-support roles in business and policy contexts. While prior benchmark studies have primarily evaluated LLMs' causal reasoning capabilities, a more fundamental epistemic dimension has been overlooked: Causal Caution, defined as the propensity to refrain from causal judgment when empirical evidence is insufficient. This study examines the systematic suppression of Causal Caution that occurs when LLMs shift from academic to practical advisory contexts. Using an evaluation rubric inspired by Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (the PCH score), we conducted experiments on four high-performance LLMs—Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT 5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro—across 480 trials. Causal Caution maintenance rates were 91.7–100.0% in academic contexts but dropped to 6.7–18.3% in practical advisory contexts (Fisher's exact test, p < .001 across all models). Furthermore, when restricted to practical prompts requesting concrete recommendations or explanatory rationales, only 1 of 200 responses (0.5%) maintained Causal Caution. A brief self-correction prompt—"Please reconsider this judgment from the perspective of causal relationships"—restored the expression of Causal Caution to maintenance rates of 71.4–100.0% (McNemar's test, p < .001 across all models). These results suggest that helpfulness-oriented response patterns may suppress the expression of Causal Caution in practical advisory contexts, with important implications for organizational governance. The findings indicate that this suppression reflects context-dependent variation in expression rather than an underlying capability limitation, suggesting that multi-agent architectures that separate proposal generation from causal auditing may offer a promising governance design.

title: Crowding Out or Crowding In? The Impact of Platform-Native LLM on Influencer Output in a Quasi-Experiment

declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported in part by the Major Program of the National Social Science Foundation of China (21&ZD118), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No.72071040), the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, and the Program of China Scholarship Council (Grant No. 202506090019).

detail.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) within social media platforms fundamentally reshapes user interactions, yet downstream consequences for content creators remain understudied. In particular, platform-native LLMs are uniquely designed to embed reference links within synthesized answers, routing user attention back to original creators. While prior literature predominantly warns that standalone AI acts as a substitute that crowds out human effort, the behavioral impact of these embedded, platform-native algorithms remains theoretically ambiguous. To address this gap, we leverage a quasi-experimental design on a major creator-driven knowledge platform. Applying a difference-indifferences framework, we find that introducing platform-native LLMs significantly increases human content production. This effect emerges immediately post-integration and persists over time, indicating a sustained operational response rather than a transitory adjustment. Further heterogeneity analyses demonstrate that the intensity of this crowd-in effect is governed by the creator's structural position. Specifically, contributors with large follower bases have cultivated deep parasocial ties with their audiences, therefore less motivated to increase their output to avoid algorithmic substitution. Meanwhile, institutional accounts and verified experts, who face severe substitution threats in objective knowledge domains, utilize their operational buffers to scale production. Our findings offer critical insights for algorithmic governance and capacity management.

detail.abstract:
This study examines how Xiaomi Auto constructs an independent brand identity within the Xiaomi Group ecosystem. Within 22 months of launch, Xiaomi Auto delivered 411,082 new cars in 2025 and has reached RMB 106.1 billion for the first time in 2025. However, this rapid success has been accompanied by a severe brand identity crisis: fundamental conflicts between inherited "Value-for-money" DNA from Xiaomi Group and aspired "premium intelligent EV" positioning.

The March 2025 Anhui accident triggered a 12x surge in 'Xiaomi Auto accident' search queries and a 0.7 correlation coefficient between negative news cycles and stock price decline. This event exemplifies the 'Speed-Credibility Trade-off' in the CBAT Model.

Utilizing PESTEL, Porter's Five Forces, SWOT, and STP frameworks, combined with Aaker's Brand Identity System and Kapferer's Identity Prism, this study reveals three critical findings: (1) structural identity tension across price anchoring, safety trust, user image, and founder dependence; (2) STP fragility—precise targeing of "New Elite" creates high conversion but conflicts with safety credibility; (3) endorsed brand dilemma—ecosystem synergies constrain brand independence.

The study contributes the Cross-Border Brand Architecture Tension (CBAT) Model, proposing a three-phase solution: strategic identity reconstruction (Speed→Safety), tactical stakeholder management (founder dependence reduction), and operational capability building.

title: Challenges and Opportunities in controlling Healthcare Provider Fraud in Public Funded Health insurance schemes in developing countries: Evidence from India

detail.title: Challenges and Opportunities in controlling Healthcare Provider Fraud in Public Funded Health insurance schemes in developing countries: Evidence from India
detail.abstract: Objectives: Of all the different types of fraud, healthcare provider fraud (HPF) not only has financial implications but can also impact patient health . This paper looks at HPF in India, which has both supply and demand-side constraints in healthcare delivery. Since 2007, several states have launched public-funded health insurance (PFHI) schemes for the poor. This paper seeks to identify the key types of HPF observed, the key reasons, and the challenges faced in fraud control. Study Design and Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 9 states and the national health agency using a survey questionnaire to analyse their perceptions on HPF. Results and Conclusion: The key reasons for health provider fraud (other than profit motive) were the low package rates set under the schemes and low footfalls in hospitals. Supply side constraints, poor public health infrastructure, low beneficiary awareness, and state capacity challenges were also important contributors.

title: Implementation of the Reporting for Better Cancer Outcomes (RBCO) Program: A system-wide multi-organisational quality improvement initiative in NSW, Australia
affiliations: Cancer Institute NSW, Cancer Institute NSW, Cancer Institute NSW, Cancer Institute NSW, Cancer Institute NSW and Monash University

detail.title: Implementation of the Reporting for Better Cancer Outcomes (RBCO) Program: A system-wide multi-organisational quality improvement initiative in NSW, Australia
detail.abstract: Background: Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI) is central to enhancing healthcare processes and outcomes. In New South Wales (NSW), the Cancer Institute NSW established Reporting for Better Cancer Outcomes (RBCO) program in 2011 to improve cancer care quality through comprehensive reporting, benchmarking, and engagement across the cancer system.,Objective: To describe the development, implementation, and integration of RBCO program using an implementation science lens, highlighting program mechanisms and system-level outcomes. Methods: A descriptive implementation study was conducted using program documentation (2011–2024), meeting records, reports, and semi-structured interviews with 31 stakeholders. Data were thematically analysed and mapped to Program Logic Framework to understand how program inputs, activities, and outputs supported implementation and contributed to system-level impact. Results: RBCO program integrated over 30 datasets and engaged more than 40 organisations, supported by state-level leadership and co-funded local leadership positions. Program activities followed RBCO CQI cycle: Plan—define objectives and secure resources; Do—deliver tailored reports, advisory groups, and forums; Study—evaluate outputs, benchmark performance, and collect feedback; Act—refine reporting, scale successful initiatives, and inform policy. Reporting expanded from 16 indicators across 16 reports (2011) to 205 indicators in 187 reports (2024 - 2025), covering prevention, screening, treatment, clinical trials, and outcomes. Conclusion: RBCO program provides a practical model of system-level CQI implementation in cancer care, across multiple organisations. By integrating data, effectively engaging clinicians and executives, and fostering leadership, RBCO demonstrates how iterative, data-driven processes can be embedded across complex healthcare systems. This implementation-focused approach offers transferable lessons for jurisdictions seeking to adopt large-scale quality improvement initiatives.

title: Blending in-office and virtual leadership behaviors to effectively lead hybrid teams
affiliations: Stetson University, University of Central Florida and University of Central Florida

detail.title: Blending in-office and virtual leadership behaviors to effectively lead hybrid teams
detail.abstract: The rapid shift from remote to hybrid work since COVID-19 has challenged team leaders to adapt their leadership behaviors to manage employees in multiple working environments. While employees generally prefer hybrid arrangements, only about 30% of their leaders’ report receiving any preparation to lead hybrid teams. Because many employees view the mandates as dismissive of their proven remote productivity and the personal benefits gained with remote work, the training gap left many team leaders unprepared to respond to the resulting employee disengagement, burnout, and frustration. Despite extensive discussions on leading hybrid workers, a 2026 London School of Economics study shows that ineffective hybrid leadership continued to hinder employee success. This article argues that hybrid work has fundamentally changed leader–member relationships and requires a new leadership approach. Indeed, limited interpersonal communications in hybrid settings often leads employees to perceive leaders as less effective, trustworthy, or supportive. While more extraverted or proactive employees tend to build stronger relationships with hybrid leaders, introverted or less assertive employees risk marginalization and reduced access to leader provided resources and advancement opportunities. Traditional in-office employees can benefit from proximity and informal interactions with leaders, but hybrid team members require greater intentionality by leaders to prevent uneven leader-member relationships. Blending in-person and virtual leadership behaviors is essential. This article offers guidelines to strengthen hybrid team effectiveness with all members.

title: Estimating Patient-Side Nursing Demand From Clinical Routine Data in Psychiatric Inpatient Care: A Multicentre Analysis of Discharge Mental Health Status
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Basel University, University Psychiatric Clinics Basel, University Psychiatric Clinics Basel and Basel University

detail.title: Estimating Patient-Side Nursing Demand From Clinical Routine Data in Psychiatric Inpatient Care: A Multicentre Analysis of Discharge Mental Health Status
detail.abstract: Background: Estimating nursing demand in psychiatric inpatient care remains challenging. Common staffing indicators may not capture within-unit changes in patient needs over time. Clinical routine data may offer a low-burden basis for estimating patient-side nursing demand, but outcome relevance is unclear.Objective: To apply two previously developed models for estimating required registered nurse (RN) hours to multicentre clinical routine data and examine whether patient exposure to high or low estimated demand was associated with discharge mental health status.Design: Retrospective longitudinal multicentre observational study using clinical routine data.Setting(s): Thirteen psychiatric hospitals in Germanspeaking Switzerland.Participants: 19,360 patient cases from 106 non-forensic adult inpatient units hospitalised January-September 2022.Methods: Two regression models — a total-score model using admission Health of the Nation Outcome Scales (HoNOS) total scores and an item-level model using severity proportions across six selected HoNOS items — estimated required RN hours for each unit and shift (three shifts per day). Patient exposure was the proportion of each stay spent under high or low estimated demand, defined by percentile thresholds and derived at the shift level and day level. The primary outcome was discharge mental health status, the HoNOS total score. Associations were examined using multilevel models adjusted for admission HoNOS. A supplementary analysis examined coercive measures.Results: Across both estimation models and all 48 threshold specifications, the direction of association was consistent: exposure to periods of high estimated required RN hours was associated with higher (worse) discharge HoNOS scores, and exposure to periods of low estimated required RN hours with lower (better) scores. The largest estimates occurred at the most extreme low-demand thresholds, up to −4.3 (5th percentile; 95% CI −5.8 to −2.8) in the total-score model and −5.1 (1st percentile; 95% CI −7.8 to −2.3), magnitudes comparable to a minimal clinically detectable change on the HoNOS. Day-level estimates showed the same directional pattern, with smaller magnitudes.Conclusions: Clinical routine data carried a consistent, outcome-relevant signal about variation in estimated nursing demand. The findings suggest that such data may support strategic staffing and capacity planning by making within-unit demand variation more visible. The underlying staffing mechanism remains to be tested using real-time data on staffing levels, skill mix, and continuity of care.

title: Treatment Targeting by Scaled Behavioral Measurement
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, affiliation not provided to SSRN, and Independent

detail.title: Treatment Targeting by Scaled Behavioral Measurement
detail.abstract: We study how behavioral economics and machine learning can jointly construct effective treatment-targeting rules. In a large field experiment at an online fashion retailer with approximately 500,000 consumers, we test a loss-framed discount message. We elicit individual loss aversion in a nested incentivized behavioral measurement experiment (N=582) and use machine learning to impute it from digital footprints. Targeting based on scaled behavioral measurement yields statistically significant revenue gains and outperforms causal forests. The results show how scaling behavioral measurement can improve algorithmic treatment assignment relative to purely data-driven approaches, especially when pilot data are unavailable, noisy, or costly.

title: Long-term Effects of US Tariff Increases on CAPDR

detail.title: Long-term Effects of US Tariff Increases on CAPDR

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In a series of declarations throughout 2025 and into 2026, the United States announced higher tariffs on nearly all imports from most countries.  The countries that make up the CAPDR region (Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama and El Salvador) are affected through sizeable direct trade linkages with the United States, and through indirect trade linkages with third countries.  This paper explores the potential long-term economic effects of these tariff increases on CAPDR using a multi-region multi-industry model of the global economy.  The modelling exercises suggest that CAPDR member countries will experience falls in real GDP to varying degrees, with the severity of the effect closely linked to direct export exposure to the United States.  The most vulnerable industries are heavily trade-exposed manufactures, although exemptions – most importantly for textiles & apparel – may provide some scope for trade diversion to offset some of the GDP losses. Although ongoing legal challenges have introduced additional uncertainty regarding the ultimate extent of tariff changes, the results in this paper will remain broadly valid providing the tariffs remain in place.
